resources.label: Microsoft Learn: Describe Azure architecture and services
Microsoft Learn: Describe Azure management and governance

flashcards.back: The delivery of computing services — servers, storage, databases, networking, software — over the internet, with pay-as-you-go pricing instead of buying and maintaining physical infrastructure.
flashcards.detail: This is the baseline definition the whole exam builds on. If a question describes 'renting' IT resources instead of owning them, it's pointing at this.

flashcards.back: A framework describing which security and management tasks the cloud provider handles versus the customer. The split shifts depending on IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS — the customer always keeps responsibility for their data and identities.
flashcards.detail: Exam trap: no matter how much Microsoft manages, the customer is never off the hook for securing their own data and accounts.

flashcards.front: Public vs. private vs. hybrid cloud
flashcards.back: Public: resources owned and shared by a third-party provider. Private: dedicated to one organization, on-premises or hosted. Hybrid: combines both, often for compliance or a gradual migration.
flashcards.detail: A healthcare org keeping patient records on-prem while running its website in Azure is a classic hybrid scenario.

flashcards.back: Pricing where you pay only for the resources you actually use, instead of a large upfront purchase.
flashcards.detail: This is the mechanism behind the CapEx-to-OpEx shift the exam likes to test.

flashcards.back: CapEx is large upfront capital spending on infrastructure you own. OpEx is ongoing operating expense — paying for what you use as you use it. Cloud computing shifts spending from CapEx toward OpEx.
flashcards.detail: If a scenario mentions avoiding a big hardware purchase, that's the CapEx-to-OpEx shift, not just 'saving money' in the abstract.

flashcards.back: A model where the provider manages the infrastructure automatically, and you're billed based on execution rather than provisioned capacity — you write code without managing servers.
flashcards.detail: Azure Functions is the canonical serverless example on this exam.

flashcards.back: Scalability is the general ability to handle more load by adding resources, manually or automatically. Elasticity specifically means resources scale up and down automatically in response to real-time demand.
flashcards.detail: Elasticity is a specific kind of scalability — the automatic, dynamic kind. Not every scalable system is elastic.

flashcards.back: Reliability means a system recovers from failures and keeps functioning. Predictability means consistent performance and cost, so you can plan capacity and budget confidently.
flashcards.detail: An unpredictable, spiky bill is a sign predictability isn't being managed well, even if the system is technically reliable.

flashcards.back: IaaS: rent infrastructure (VMs, storage, networking), you manage the OS and up. PaaS: rent a platform, you manage just your app and data. SaaS: rent a finished application, you just use it.
flashcards.detail: Microsoft 365 is the textbook SaaS example. Azure App Service is the textbook PaaS example.

flashcards.back: Moving from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS gives you more that's managed for you, but less direct control. Match the scenario's control needs to the right type.
flashcards.detail: If a question stresses 'wants full control of the OS,' that's IaaS. If it stresses 'just wants the app to work,' that's SaaS.

flashcards.back: A discounted pricing option for unused Azure capacity, in exchange for accepting that the VM can be evicted with little notice if Azure needs that capacity back.
flashcards.detail: The trade-off — big discount for interruption risk — makes Spot the right answer for low-priority, interruption-tolerant workloads, never for anything mission-critical.

flashcards.back: A region is a set of datacenters in a geographic area. Region pairs are two regions in the same geography, at least 300 miles apart, used for disaster recovery — updates roll out to only one region in a pair at a time.
flashcards.detail: The 300-mile / same-geography detail is a specific fact the exam likes to test directly. Remember the exceptions: not every region has a pair (Italy North, Poland Central, and Israel Central rely on availability zones and geo-redundant storage), and Brazil South is paired one way with South Central US, outside its geography.

flashcards.back: Physically and logically isolated Azure regions for specific compliance or legal needs, operated separately from global Azure. Examples are the U.S. government regions (Azure Government) and the China regions run through a partnership with 21Vianet.
flashcards.detail: These exist specifically so certain government or regulatory data never touches the general commercial cloud.

flashcards.back: Physically separate datacenters within an Azure region, each with independent power, cooling, and networking, used to protect against a single datacenter failing.
flashcards.detail: Region = geography. Availability zone = specific datacenter within that geography. An availability zone does NOT protect against a whole region going down.

flashcards.back: A resource is any deployable item in Azure, like a VM or database. A resource group is a logical container holding related resources that you deploy, manage, and delete as a group — and can contain resources from more than one region.
flashcards.detail: Deleting a resource group deletes everything inside it — a common 'what happens if' exam scenario.

flashcards.back: A logical container that groups resource groups together, tied to billing and access management. An organization can have multiple subscriptions for different departments or environments.
flashcards.detail: Subscriptions sit above resource groups and below management groups in the hierarchy.

flashcards.back: Containers that group multiple subscriptions together, letting you apply governance policies, like Azure Policy or RBAC, across many subscriptions at once.
flashcards.detail: Useful for a large org that wants one security policy applied to every subscription without configuring each one separately. Deleting a management group does not delete the subscriptions inside it.

flashcards.back: From broadest to narrowest: management groups, then subscriptions, then resource groups, then individual resources. Settings applied higher up flow down and compound going down.
flashcards.detail: A policy added at a lower scope can make things more restrictive than the parent required, but never less.

flashcards.back: VMs: full control, you manage the OS. Containers: lightweight, package an app with its dependencies, more portable than a VM. Functions: run small pieces of code on demand, fully serverless.
flashcards.detail: As you move VM → container → function, management overhead drops and portability/scalability generally goes up.

flashcards.back: Scale Sets automatically add or remove identical VMs based on demand or schedule. Availability sets group VMs so they don't all update or fail at once, within one datacenter. Azure Virtual Desktop delivers virtual desktops or apps to users.
flashcards.detail: Scale Sets are about scaling out. Availability sets are about not losing everything at once during maintenance or a single-datacenter failure — not a whole-region failure.

flashcards.back: Web apps (App Service, PaaS, easiest), containers (more portable, more control), and virtual machines (most control, most management overhead) — pick based on how much you want to manage.
flashcards.detail: App Service is the go-to answer when a scenario just needs 'a website, minimal management.'

flashcards.back: A virtual network (VNet) is a private network in Azure. Subnets divide it into smaller segments. Peering connects VNets. Azure DNS resolves names. VPN Gateway and ExpressRoute connect on-premises networks to Azure.
flashcards.detail: VPN Gateway travels over the public internet, encrypted. ExpressRoute is a private, dedicated connection — and is NOT encrypted by default, since it relies on the private connection itself.

flashcards.back: A public endpoint is reachable over the internet. A private endpoint gives a resource a private IP inside your VNet, so traffic never leaves the Microsoft network.
flashcards.detail: Private endpoints are the answer whenever a scenario wants to reduce internet exposure for a resource like a database.

flashcards.back: Blob (unstructured data), Files (managed file shares), Queue (messaging), Disk (block volumes for VMs), and Table (NoSQL key-value) storage are the core Azure Storage services. Blob, Files, Queue, and Table data live inside a storage account.
flashcards.detail: The storage account is the top-level container; blobs, files, queues, and tables live inside it. Azure Disk storage provides the managed disks that back Azure VMs.

flashcards.back: Hot, Cool, Cold, and Archive tiers balance storage cost against access speed and retrieval cost — Hot is most expensive to store but cheapest/fastest to access, Archive is the opposite.
flashcards.detail: Archive tier data can take hours to retrieve — a scenario needing frequent, fast access should never point to Archive, but one needing cheap, rarely-touched long-term storage does.

flashcards.back: LRS keeps copies in one datacenter. ZRS spreads copies across availability zones in one region. GRS/GZRS copies to a secondary paired region for disaster recovery. RA-GRS (or RA-GZRS) adds read access to that secondary region even before a failover happens.
flashcards.detail: Plain GRS isn't readable from the secondary region until failover — the read-access ('RA-') variants are the ones you can read from directly, at any time.

flashcards.front: AzCopy vs. Storage Explorer vs. Azure File Sync
flashcards.back: AzCopy is a command-line tool for scripted, one-time or bulk file transfers into Azure Storage. Storage Explorer is a GUI tool for browsing and managing storage data. Azure File Sync keeps an on-premises file server continuously synchronized with an Azure file share.
flashcards.detail: File Sync is the odd one out — it's ongoing synchronization, not a one-time transfer tool like the other two.

flashcards.front: Azure Migrate vs. Azure Data Box
flashcards.back: Azure Migrate assesses and migrates on-premises servers and workloads into Azure, typically over the network. Azure Data Box is a physical device shipped to you for transferring very large datasets when network transfer would be too slow.
flashcards.detail: If a scenario mentions terabytes of data and a slow internet connection, that's pointing at Data Box, not Migrate.

flashcards.back: Microsoft's cloud-based identity and access management service, formerly Azure Active Directory. Manages users, groups, and access to apps and resources.
flashcards.detail: Renamed from Azure AD — expect both names to appear in materials, but Entra ID is the current name.

flashcards.back: Single sign-on: one login for multiple apps. Multifactor authentication: a second verification step beyond a password. Passwordless: authentication without a password at all, like a security key or authenticator app.
flashcards.detail: These three get tested as distinct concepts — don't conflate MFA with passwordless, they're different approaches.

flashcards.back: Lets people outside your organization, like partners or customers, sign in using their own identities rather than you creating them a new account in your directory.
flashcards.detail: This is the answer when a scenario mentions collaborating with an outside company without issuing them internal accounts. Microsoft Entra External ID is the current product family for this.

flashcards.back: Policies that grant or block access based on conditions like user location, device compliance state, or risk level — for example, requiring MFA only when signing in from an unfamiliar location.
flashcards.detail: Conditional Access is about the conditions under which access is allowed — not just location, but device state, app, and risk level too — distinct from RBAC which is about what access is granted.

flashcards.back: Role-based access control assigns permissions to users, groups, or applications at a specific scope — management group, subscription, resource group, or resource — following least-privilege principles.
flashcards.detail: RBAC answers 'what can this identity do,' Conditional Access answers 'under what conditions can they do it.'

flashcards.back: A security model that assumes no user or device is trusted by default, even inside the network perimeter — every request is verified based on identity, device, and context.
flashcards.detail: "Never trust, always verify" is the one-line summary. This is the answer when a scenario shows a perimeter breach that still fails to grant access.

flashcards.back: A layered security strategy — physical, identity, perimeter, network, compute, application, and data layers — so that if one layer is breached, others still protect the resource.
flashcards.detail: Think of it as concentric rings of security around your data, not a single wall — related to, but distinct from, Zero Trust.

flashcards.back: A tool that assesses your security posture across Azure, hybrid, and other-cloud resources and gives recommendations to improve it, plus threat protection for workloads.
flashcards.detail: Defender for Cloud is narrower and security-specific. Azure Advisor is broader, covering cost, reliability, and performance too.

flashcards.back: An automatically-managed Entra ID identity for an Azure resource, like a VM or Function, letting it authenticate to other Azure services without embedding credentials in code.
flashcards.detail: This is the answer whenever a scenario wants passwordless, credential-free authentication between Azure services.

flashcards.back: Resource type, usage/consumption, region, and licensing all affect what you pay in Azure.
flashcards.detail: Region matters because pricing varies by datacenter location — a detail that's easy to overlook.

flashcards.back: The Pricing calculator estimates the cost of Azure resources you plan to use. The Total Cost of Ownership calculator compares your current on-premises infrastructure cost against running it in Azure over time.
flashcards.detail: If a scenario asks 'should we move to the cloud at all,' that's the TCO calculator. If it asks 'what will this specific setup cost,' that's the Pricing calculator.

flashcards.back: Name/value pairs attached to resources for organizing and tracking, like by department or environment — useful for cost reporting and filtering in Cost Management.
flashcards.detail: Tags don't affect how a resource functions, only how it's organized and reported on.

flashcards.back: A unified data governance service that helps you discover, classify, and protect sensitive data across your organization, including hybrid, non-Azure sources.
flashcards.detail: Purview is about knowing what data you have and how sensitive it is, not about access control itself.

flashcards.back: Enforces organizational rules on resources, for example requiring a specific region or blocking a VM size, and evaluates and reports on compliance — it can even deny non-compliant deployments outright.
flashcards.detail: Policy governs how resources must be configured. RBAC governs who can act on them — a distinction the exam tests directly.

flashcards.back: A Delete lock blocks deletion only. A Read-only lock blocks both deletion and modification. Both override a user's normal permissions, regardless of what RBAC otherwise allows.
flashcards.detail: Exam trap: a Delete lock will NOT stop someone from modifying a resource's settings — only a Read-only lock does that.

flashcards.back: The Azure portal is the web GUI. Cloud Shell is a browser-based command line, no local install needed. Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell are command-line tools installed locally for scripting — four ways to manage the same resources.
flashcards.detail: Cloud Shell running in the browser is what distinguishes it from CLI/PowerShell installed on your own machine.

flashcards.back: IaC means defining infrastructure in code or config files instead of manual clicks, so deployments are repeatable and version-controllable. ARM templates are Azure's native JSON format for declaring what resources to deploy.
flashcards.detail: Repeatability and version control are the key benefits IaC brings that clicking through the portal doesn't.

flashcards.back: A free tool that analyzes your resource configuration and usage, then gives personalized recommendations across cost, security, reliability, operational excellence, and performance.
flashcards.detail: Advisor is broad (cost, security, reliability, operational excellence, performance). Defender for Cloud is specifically security-focused.

flashcards.back: Collects and analyzes telemetry from your Azure resources — Log Analytics stores and queries logs, Azure Monitor alerts notify you of conditions, and Application Insights monitors live applications.
flashcards.detail: Log Analytics is the query/storage layer inside Azure Monitor, not a separate standalone product.

flashcards.back: Extends Azure management tools, like Azure Policy and RBAC, to resources outside Azure — on-premises servers, other clouds, or edge devices — managed with the same tools as native Azure resources.
flashcards.detail: Arc is the answer whenever a scenario wants 'one pane of glass' for Azure plus non-Azure infrastructure.

flashcards.back: Reports on the health of the Azure platform itself — like an ongoing outage in a region — separate from the health of your own specific resources.
flashcards.detail: Service Health = is Azure itself having a problem. Azure Monitor = is my stuff having a problem. Different questions, different tools.

flashcards.back: Microsoft's formal, measurable commitment to an uptime or performance target for a service, such as 99.9% monthly uptime, backed by service credits if the target is missed.
flashcards.detail: An SLA is a commitment with a financial remedy, not a guarantee of zero downtime — a distinction the exam tests directly.

flashcards.back: The effective SLA of a solution built from multiple dependent services. Chaining services in sequence multiplies their individual uptime percentages, producing a LOWER composite SLA than any single component. Adding redundant, independent components in parallel can raise the composite SLA above any one component's own figure.
flashcards.detail: Exam trap: depending on more services in sequence generally lowers your overall SLA, even though each individual piece still meets its own target.

flashcards.back: Basic support is free and included with every subscription, covering billing and subscription questions. Paid tiers — Developer, Standard, and Professional Direct — add technical support with progressively faster guaranteed response times for production issues. Microsoft Unified support (the current name for what was once called Premier) sits above these as a broader, account-managed enterprise offering rather than just another response-time tier.
flashcards.detail: Basic support alone has no response-time commitment for a production-down technical issue — that requires a paid tier.

flashcards.back: A licensing benefit that lets you apply existing on-premises Windows Server or SQL Server licenses (with active Software Assurance or an eligible subscription) toward the cost of running those workloads in Azure, instead of paying for a new license.
flashcards.detail: A separate cost lever from Reservations or Spot pricing — it reduces the licensing portion of the bill, not the underlying compute rate.

flashcards.back: A set of allow/deny security rules that filter inbound and outbound network traffic to Azure resources, based on source/destination IP, port, and protocol — applied at a subnet or an individual network interface.
flashcards.detail: NSGs are the baseline traffic-filtering tool on this exam; Azure Firewall is a more advanced managed alternative, but NSGs are the AZ-900-level answer.

flashcards.back: Azure Load Balancer works at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP), distributing traffic by IP and port with no awareness of content. Application Gateway works at Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS), routing by URL path or host header, and can add a Web Application Firewall.
flashcards.detail: If a scenario mentions routing by URL path or needing a WAF, that's Application Gateway, not Load Balancer.

flashcards.back: A managed Kubernetes service for orchestrating, scaling, and self-healing groups of containers across a cluster of nodes — Azure manages the control plane, you manage your workloads.
flashcards.detail: AKS is the answer for orchestrating many containers at scale; Azure Container Instances is the answer for running one or a few standalone containers quickly, with no orchestration layer.

flashcards.back: A concise, domain-specific language for defining Azure infrastructure as code, which compiles down to standard ARM template JSON and deploys through the same Azure Resource Manager.
flashcards.detail: Bicep is Microsoft's current recommended way to author IaC on Azure — easier to read and write than raw ARM JSON, but functionally equivalent underneath.

flashcards.back: A deployment strategy that deliberately uses more than one public cloud provider, for example Azure alongside another provider, to avoid depending on a single vendor or to use each provider's strongest services.
flashcards.detail: Distinct from hybrid cloud: hybrid mixes on-premises/private infrastructure with public cloud; multi-cloud mixes two or more public cloud providers.

flashcards.front: Azure CDN vs. Azure Front Door
flashcards.back: Azure CDN caches static content at edge points-of-presence close to users to cut latency. Azure Front Door adds global HTTP(S) load balancing, path-based routing, and an optional Web Application Firewall on top of an edge network, for full web-application delivery, not just static caching.
flashcards.detail: If a scenario needs only 'serve images/video faster worldwide,' that's CDN. If it also needs routing logic or a WAF at the edge, that's Front Door, which is also where Microsoft is steering new work: Azure CDN Standard from Microsoft (classic) retires on September 30, 2027 and no longer supports creating profiles or onboarding new domains, and Azure CDN from Edgio was retired on January 15, 2025.

flashcards.back: Microsoft Cost Management (formerly Azure Cost Management) is the set of tools for analyzing spend (cost analysis), setting alerts and budgets, and, with the Billing tools alongside it, viewing and paying invoices, across one or more subscriptions.
flashcards.detail: This is where the factors that drive Azure costs show up as real, analyzable numbers, and where the estimates from the Pricing and TCO calculators get checked against what you actually spend.

flashcards.back: A pre-configured environment — subscriptions, management groups, policy, and a network baseline already in place — that a new workload lands into, instead of starting from a blank subscription every time.
flashcards.detail: A landing zone bakes governance into the resource hierarchy up front, so a new workload inherits compliant Azure Policy and Azure RBAC instead of every project reinventing it.

flashcards.back: Microsoft's guidance for evaluating a workload against five pillars — reliability, security, cost optimization, operational excellence, and performance efficiency — used to weigh trade-offs against each other rather than optimizing just one in isolation.
flashcards.detail: Azure Advisor's recommendations are aligned with these same pillars and are generated automatically from your actual resources, flagging where a workload falls short.

flashcards.back: Lets a service provider or central IT team manage resources across multiple Azure tenants from within their own tenant, without switching directories or needing a separate guest account in each customer's tenant.
flashcards.detail: This is specifically for cross-tenant management at scale — an MSP managing dozens of customer tenants is the classic scenario, distinct from Azure RBAC, which governs access within a single tenant.

flashcards.back: A service for securely storing and tightly controlling access to secrets, encryption keys, and certificates, so they never sit hardcoded in application source code. An app typically authenticates to it using a managed identity rather than an embedded credential, with access to individual secrets still governed through Microsoft Entra ID and Azure RBAC like any other resource.
flashcards.detail: Key Vault is the answer whenever a scenario wants to eliminate a hardcoded connection string or API key from source code entirely.

flashcards.back: A managed service that provides secure RDP and SSH access to virtual machines directly through the Azure portal over TLS, without needing a public endpoint on the VM itself or a client-side VPN. It works alongside a network security group (NSG) rather than replacing it — the NSG still filters what traffic is allowed to reach the VM's subnet in the first place.
flashcards.detail: Bastion is the answer whenever a scenario wants to remove a VM's exposed public RDP/SSH port while still allowing administrators to connect.

flashcards.back: A managed service that takes scheduled, application-consistent backups of Azure VMs, SQL databases, and other workloads into a Recovery Services vault. Those recovery points are protected by the vault's own storage redundancy setting — LRS, ZRS, or GRS (the default) — so the backup data can survive a datacenter failure, or with GRS a regional one.
flashcards.detail: Azure Backup protects data that already exists by restoring it after loss or corruption; it's a different job from Site Recovery, which keeps a whole workload running by replicating it to fail over to.

flashcards.back: Designing a workload so it stays accessible with as little downtime as possible, usually by running redundant components and spreading them across separate failure boundaries such as availability zones.
flashcards.detail: Two VMs in different availability zones behind a load balancer is a high availability design. It is measured as an uptime percentage, which is exactly what an SLA promises.

flashcards.back: The ability of a system to keep working correctly when one of its components fails, usually because redundant parts take over automatically. The goal is that users notice no interruption.
flashcards.detail: Exam angle: high availability aims to minimize downtime, while fault tolerance aims to avoid a visible failure altogether. Spreading VMs across zones supports both.

flashcards.back: The plan and tooling for restoring workloads and data after a major disruption, such as the loss of a whole datacenter or region. It is a different job from handling small, routine component failures.
flashcards.detail: Replicating VMs to a second region with Azure Site Recovery is disaster recovery. Availability zones cover a datacenter failure but not a regional outage.

flashcards.front: Recovery time objective (RTO) and recovery point objective (RPO)
flashcards.back: RTO is the longest acceptable time to restore a service after a failure. RPO is the largest amount of data loss, measured in time, that is acceptable. Together they set how much redundancy and backup a workload needs.
flashcards.detail: Nightly backups mean an RPO of up to 24 hours. A business that cannot lose more than five minutes of data needs far more frequent replication than that.

flashcards.back: A pricing option where you commit to specific resources, such as a VM size in a region, for one or three years in return for a discount of up to 72 percent compared with pay-as-you-go.
flashcards.detail: Best for steady, predictable workloads that run all the time, like a production database VM. It saves nothing on usage you stop needing, so it is wrong for short-lived or unpredictable use.

flashcards.back: A pricing option where you commit to a fixed hourly spend for one or three years and get discounted rates, up to 65 percent, on eligible compute usage across services and regions without tying it to one VM size.
flashcards.detail: Choose it over a reservation when VM sizes or regions change often. The trade-off is a slightly lower maximum discount in exchange for flexibility.

flashcards.back: An architecture that splits an application into small, independent services, each built, deployed, and scaled on its own and communicating over well-defined interfaces. Containers are a common way to run them.
flashcards.detail: Updating a checkout service without redeploying the product catalog is the payoff. Azure Container Apps and AKS are common homes for microservices.

flashcards.back: Automatically adding or removing resources in response to load, based on metrics or a schedule. Scaling out and in changes the number of instances. Scaling up and down changes the size of one instance.
flashcards.detail: A web tier that adds instances during a sale and removes them afterward shows elasticity, which keeps cost tied to demand. Azure Monitor autoscale drives it for scale sets and App Service.

flashcards.back: A cloud provider operating at huge size buys hardware, power, and capacity in bulk and spreads costs across many customers, so each customer's unit price can be lower than running the same infrastructure alone.
flashcards.detail: It is one reason cloud pricing can beat on-premises costs for similar capacity, and part of why the consumption model works for small organizations.

flashcards.back: The benefit that cloud resources are easier to run and control: you manage the cloud with automated scaling, templates, and monitoring, and manage in the cloud through portals, command-line tools, and APIs.
flashcards.detail: Deploying identical environments from a template, then monitoring them from a single portal, is manageability. It is a different benefit from reliability or scalability.

flashcards.back: A logical grouping of VMs that Azure spreads across fault domains, separate racks with their own power and network, and update domains, groups rebooted one at a time during planned maintenance. It protects within a single datacenter.
flashcards.detail: A single VM has a lower SLA than two or more VMs in an availability set, and zones give an even higher one. An availability set does not survive the loss of the whole datacenter.

flashcards.back: A group of load-balanced VMs created from the same configuration that Azure can grow or shrink automatically on demand or on a schedule. They are meant for scalable, highly available applications.
flashcards.detail: A web tier that needs more instances during weekday peaks is a scale set scenario. It is about adding identical VMs, not about spreading failures across racks like an availability set.

flashcards.back: A platform-as-a-service offering for hosting web apps, APIs, and mobile backends. Azure manages the operating system, patching, and load balancing, and it supports several languages and containers.
flashcards.detail: App Service is the usual answer when a scenario needs a website with minimal infrastructure management. You supply code or a container, not a VM.

flashcards.back: A way to run a container in Azure without managing a VM or an orchestrator, started in seconds and billed for the time it runs. It suits simple, short-lived, or single-container workloads.
flashcards.detail: Running one batch job in a container and then letting it exit fits Container Instances. Orchestrating many containers at scale is the job of AKS instead.

flashcards.back: A serverless platform for running microservices and containerized apps, built on Kubernetes but hiding the cluster. It handles HTTP ingress and scales each app, down to zero replicas when idle.
flashcards.detail: Choose it for microservices when you do not want to manage Kubernetes. If a scenario needs direct access to the Kubernetes API or node pools, that points to AKS.

flashcards.back: An event-driven, serverless compute service that runs small pieces of code when triggered by something like an HTTP request, a timer, or a queue message. On the Consumption plan you pay per execution.
flashcards.detail: Resizing an image each time one is uploaded to Blob Storage is a typical Function. You write the code and never provision or patch a server.

flashcards.back: A gateway that sends encrypted traffic between an Azure virtual network and an on-premises network (site-to-site) or individual devices (point-to-site) across the public internet.
flashcards.detail: It is cheaper and quicker to set up than ExpressRoute, but traffic crosses the internet, so performance is less predictable. Encryption is built in.

flashcards.back: A private, dedicated connection from an on-premises network to Azure through a connectivity provider, which does not cross the public internet. It offers more reliable, predictable latency and high bandwidth.
flashcards.detail: Private does not mean encrypted: add an IPsec VPN over the circuit or MACsec to encrypt. Pick ExpressRoute for consistent performance, VPN Gateway for a quicker, cheaper link.

flashcards.back: A service for hosting DNS zones and records on Azure's global network, so a domain's names resolve using Azure infrastructure. Private DNS zones resolve names only inside linked virtual networks.
flashcards.detail: A private zone lets VMs find each other by name inside a VNet without exposing those names to the internet. A public zone answers queries from anywhere.

flashcards.back: A connection between two virtual networks that lets their resources talk using private IP addresses over the Microsoft backbone, as if they were one network. It works within a region and across regions.
flashcards.detail: Peering is not transitive: if A peers with B and B with C, A and C still cannot talk unless they are also peered. It also needs no gateway or public internet.

flashcards.back: A DNS-based traffic load balancer that directs users to the best of several endpoints, possibly in different regions, using methods like priority, weighted, performance, or geographic routing.
flashcards.detail: Because it works at the DNS level, it steers clients but does not proxy the traffic. It suits regional failover, while Front Door adds edge routing and a web application firewall.

flashcards.back: Azure's object storage for large amounts of unstructured data such as images, video, backups, and logs, accessible over HTTP or HTTPS. Data can sit in the Hot, Cool, Cold, or Archive access tier.
flashcards.detail: Storing website images or long-term backups is a Blob scenario. It is the answer for unstructured files, not for a shared drive that users mount like a network folder.

flashcards.back: Fully managed file shares in the cloud reachable through the SMB protocol, and the NFS protocol on supported share types. They can be mounted at the same time from Azure or on-premises machines.
flashcards.detail: Replacing an on-premises file server with a mountable cloud share is Azure Files. Add Azure File Sync to keep a local server and the share continuously in step.

flashcards.back: A fully managed, globally distributed NoSQL database offering very low latency and automatic replication to multiple regions. It supports several APIs and data models.
flashcards.detail: A worldwide app that needs fast reads and writes close to users in every region fits Cosmos DB. A traditional relational workload points to Azure SQL Database.

flashcards.back: A managed relational database service built on the SQL Server engine. Azure handles patching, backups, and built-in high availability, so you manage only the data and the schema.
flashcards.detail: Moving a relational app to Azure SQL Database trades control for less administration. Running SQL Server on a VM instead keeps full control but leaves patching to you.

flashcards.back: A tool that synchronizes identities from an on-premises Active Directory to Microsoft Entra ID, so users can sign in to cloud and on-premises resources with the same identity. This setup is called hybrid identity.
flashcards.detail: A company keeping on-premises Active Directory while moving to Microsoft 365 uses it so staff do not need a second set of accounts.

flashcards.back: A firewall that inspects HTTP and HTTPS traffic to protect web applications from common attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting. In Azure it is an option on Application Gateway and Front Door.
flashcards.detail: A network security group filters by IP and port only, so blocking a malicious request body needs a WAF. It is the layer 7 protection for web apps.

flashcards.back: Azure's deployment and management layer. Every request from the portal, CLI, PowerShell, SDKs, or REST APIs goes through it, so authentication, RBAC, policies, and locks are applied consistently however you manage resources.
flashcards.detail: ARM templates and Bicep deploy through it. That is why a resource created in the CLI immediately shows up in the portal with the same permissions.

flashcards.back: A service that reports the health of an individual resource, such as one VM or database, and its recent history, helping you tell whether unavailability comes from the Azure platform or from your own configuration.
flashcards.detail: Service Health tells you about platform events affecting your regions and services. Resource Health tells you about your one specific resource.

flashcards.back: The store inside Azure Monitor where log data from many resources is collected and queried using Kusto Query Language (KQL). It is the place to search and analyze logs, not a separate product from Monitor.
flashcards.detail: Sending VM and application logs to one workspace lets you run a single query across all of them. Alerts can then be built from those queries.

flashcards.back: An Azure Monitor feature for application performance monitoring. It tracks request rates, response times, failures, dependencies, and user behavior in live web applications so developers can find and diagnose problems.
flashcards.detail: Use it when a scenario asks why a deployed app is slow or throwing errors. Azure Monitor metrics on the VM host would not show failing application requests.

flashcards.front: Azure Monitor alerts and action groups
flashcards.back: An alert rule watches metrics, logs, or activity events and fires when a condition is met. It then calls an action group, a reusable set of notifications and automated actions such as email, SMS, webhooks, or a Function.
flashcards.detail: An alert for CPU above 90 percent that emails the on-call team is one rule plus one action group. The same group can be reused by many rules.

flashcards.back: A policy's effect decides what happens to a non-compliant resource. Audit only flags it, Deny blocks the request, and Modify changes properties such as adding a tag. DeployIfNotExists deploys a related resource.
flashcards.detail: Audit reports without stopping anyone. Existing resources are only flagged, not changed, unless a remediation task is run. Deny only stops new or updated resources.

flashcards.back: Owner has full access and can grant access to others. Contributor can create and manage resources but cannot grant access. Reader can only view resources. User Access Administrator manages access only.
flashcards.detail: A developer who must deploy resources but not assign permissions gets Contributor. An auditor who must only look gets Reader. Both are applied through Azure RBAC at a chosen scope.

flashcards.front: Microsoft Cloud Adoption Framework for Azure
flashcards.back: Microsoft's guidance, best practices, and tools for adopting the cloud, organized into Strategy, Plan, Ready, Adopt, Govern, Secure, and Manage. It covers the whole journey, from business case to day-two operations.
flashcards.detail: Landing zones come from the Ready phase. Do not confuse it with the Well-Architected Framework, which guides the design quality of a single workload.

flashcards.back: Microsoft's standard agreement for buying Azure and other Microsoft cloud services directly. Costs are organized under a billing account, with billing profiles for invoices and invoice sections for grouping charges.
flashcards.detail: Pay-as-you-go under an MCA has no upfront volume commitment and is billed as usage occurs. That contrasts with a commitment-based enterprise purchasing agreement.

flashcards.back: Public preview features can be tried by any customer before official release, may change, and are excluded from SLAs. General availability means a service is released for production use and covered by its SLA and full support.
flashcards.detail: Do not run mission-critical workloads on a preview feature. A private preview is invitation-only and is not covered by Azure support plans.

flashcards.back: Vertical scaling changes the size of a resource: scale up by adding CPU or RAM to an existing VM, or scale down by trimming them. Horizontal scaling changes the number of resources: scale out by adding VMs or containers, or scale in by removing them.
flashcards.detail: Bigger or smaller box versus more or fewer boxes. Either can be manual or automatic, but autoscale rules usually work horizontally by adding or removing instances.

flashcards.front: Security and governance benefits of the cloud
flashcards.back: Templates and policies help every deployed resource meet technical and regulatory standards, and can be updated at scale when standards change. Cloud-based auditing flags resources that drift out of compliance and suggests mitigation. Large providers are also well placed to absorb attacks such as distributed denial of service (DDoS).
flashcards.detail: How much patching Microsoft handles still depends on the service model: you patch the guest OS on IaaS, while PaaS and SaaS shift most of that work to the provider. Governance set up early keeps the cloud footprint secure and well managed.

flashcards.back: In every cloud model the customer stays responsible for its data and information, the devices allowed to connect, and the accounts and identities of its people, services, and devices. The provider always owns the physical datacenter, physical network, and physical hosts.
flashcards.detail: Operating systems, network controls, applications, and identity infrastructure move between customer and provider depending on IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS. Even in SaaS the customer still owns data and who has access to it.

flashcards.back: A service that lets an organization already running VMware workloads in a private cloud run those same VMware workloads in Azure, with Azure's integration and scalability, instead of re-platforming each VM.
flashcards.detail: Choose it when the scenario stresses an existing VMware estate and a move to a public or hybrid cloud with minimal change. Azure Arc, by contrast, manages resources where they already run; it does not move them.

flashcards.back: A free trial subscription includes credit to spend within the first 30 days, a set of products that are free for 12 months, and more than 25 products that are always free, subject to resource and region availability.
flashcards.detail: The credit does not last 12 months: it must be spent in the first 30 days, while the 12-month benefit applies to specific free products. Usage beyond the free allowances is billed normally.

flashcards.back: A region is one or more datacenters connected by a high-capacity, low-latency network, usually inside a large metropolitan area. A geography, such as the United States or Europe, is a data residency boundary that holds one or more regions. You choose a region for most resources; you never choose an individual datacenter.
flashcards.detail: A few services are global and need no region choice, including Microsoft Entra ID, Azure Traffic Manager, and Azure DNS. Some VM sizes and storage types are only offered in certain regions.

flashcards.back: Services that use availability zones fall into three groups. Zonal services are pinned by you to one zone, like VMs, managed disks, and IP addresses. Zone-redundant services replicate across zones automatically, like zone-redundant storage and SQL Database. Non-regional services are always available from Azure geographies and survive both zone and region outages.
flashcards.detail: Every availability zone-enabled region has at least three separate zones. Zonal resources give you the placement control but also the job of spreading copies yourself, and duplicating across zones can add cost.

flashcards.back: Most regions are paired in both directions, but not all. Brazil South is paired one way with South Central US, which is outside its geography, and South Central US is not paired back. Some regions, such as Italy North, Poland Central, and Israel Central, have no traditional pair and rely on availability zones and geo-redundant storage for resiliency.
flashcards.detail: A pair does not fail workloads over for you. Not every service replicates automatically between paired regions, so recovery and replication often have to be configured by the customer.

flashcards.front: Azure Government and Azure operated by 21Vianet
flashcards.back: Two examples of sovereign regions, Azure instances isolated from the main Azure cloud for compliance or legal reasons. US Gov and US DoD regions are physically and logically network-isolated for U.S. government agencies and partners and are operated by screened U.S. personnel. The China regions are run through a partnership with 21Vianet, so Microsoft does not directly maintain those datacenters.
flashcards.detail: Sovereign cloud regions work like other regions but often offer a more limited set of services and features.

flashcards.back: B-series is burstable and cost-efficient, D-series is general purpose, E-series is memory optimized, F-series is compute optimized, M-series has a very large memory footprint, L-series is storage optimized, and N-series is GPU enabled. In a name like D2s_v5, D is the family, 2 is the vCPU count, s means Premium SSD support, and v5 is the hardware generation.
flashcards.detail: Pick the family that matches how the workload behaves, then the size that meets performance needs. Dev/test with occasional CPU spikes points to B-series; in-memory databases point to E-series.

flashcards.front: Resources required for a virtual machine
flashcards.back: A VM needs a size (cores and RAM), storage disks, and networking. Disks hold the operating system and any data. Networking means a virtual network and subnet, a network interface, an optional public IP address, and port rules such as an NSG.
flashcards.detail: Deleting a VM does not always delete these companions: orphaned disks, network interfaces, and public IPs can keep appearing on the bill until they are removed too.

flashcards.back: A desktop and application virtualization service that delivers Windows desktops and apps hosted in Azure to users on many kinds of devices. It integrates with Microsoft Entra ID and supports both single-session and multi-session Windows.
flashcards.detail: It suits distributed or shift-based teams that need the same centrally managed desktop and keep data in Azure rather than on local devices. Azure Bastion, by comparison, is for administrators reaching VMs.

flashcards.back: App Service hosts web apps, API apps, WebJobs, and mobile app back ends on the same infrastructure, on Windows or Linux. WebJobs run a program or script, such as a nightly job, in the context of a web, API, or mobile app, on a schedule or by a trigger.
flashcards.detail: Built-in scaling, load balancing, and automated deployment from GitHub, Azure DevOps, or any Git repo come with the platform, so you manage only the app.

flashcards.back: A service endpoint lets resources in a subnet reach an Azure service such as Storage or SQL Database over an optimized route on the Azure backbone, and lets you restrict that service to your virtual networks. A private endpoint gives the service a private IP address from your own virtual network's address space.
flashcards.detail: Microsoft recommends Private Link and private endpoints for most new designs. The giveaway for a private endpoint is the phrase 'a private IP address inside our virtual network'.

flashcards.back: Azure VPN Gateway supports three connection types: site-to-site links an on-premises VPN device to the Azure gateway, point-to-site lets one client computer start an encrypted connection into a virtual network, and network-to-network connects two virtual networks. All traffic is encrypted inside a tunnel across the internet.
flashcards.detail: The gateway lives in a dedicated subnet and a virtual network can have only one VPN gateway. By default it runs as two instances in active/standby; active/active and zone-redundant gateways raise availability.

flashcards.front: Routing and filtering traffic in a virtual network
flashcards.back: By default Azure routes between subnets, connected networks, on-premises networks, and the internet. Route tables and user-defined routes override that path, and BGP can propagate on-premises routes. Network security groups filter by source, destination, port, and protocol, and network virtual appliances run functions such as a firewall.
flashcards.detail: Routing decides where packets go; filtering decides whether they are allowed. An NSG filters, a route table steers.

flashcards.front: ExpressRoute Global Reach and what still uses the internet
flashcards.back: ExpressRoute Global Reach connects your on-premises sites to each other through their ExpressRoute circuits over the Microsoft network, such as an Asia office to a European datacenter. Even with ExpressRoute, DNS queries, certificate revocation list checks, and Azure Content Delivery Network requests still travel over the public internet.
flashcards.detail: ExpressRoute also reaches Microsoft 365 and Dynamics 365, uses BGP for dynamic routing, and has built-in redundancy at each peering location.

flashcards.back: Standard general-purpose v2 supports blobs (including Data Lake Storage), queues, tables, and files with every redundancy option, and is recommended for most scenarios. Premium block blobs suit high transaction rates and consistently low latency. Premium file shares are for Azure Files and support SMB and NFS. Premium page blobs are for page blobs only. Premium accounts support only LRS and ZRS (page blobs only LRS).
flashcards.detail: A storage account name must be 3 to 24 characters, using lowercase letters and numbers only, and must be unique across Azure.

flashcards.front: Azure Disk storage and Queue storage
flashcards.back: Disk storage (managed disks) provides block-level volumes for Azure VMs, with Azure handling the underlying resilience. Queue storage holds large numbers of messages, up to 64 KB each, for reliable asynchronous messaging between application components, often paired with Azure Functions.
flashcards.detail: With these two, the core Azure Storage data services are Blobs, Files, Queues, Disks, and Tables.

flashcards.front: Blob access tier minimum stays and scope
flashcards.back: Cool is for data stored at least 30 days, Cold at least 90 days, and Archive at least 180 days with flexible latency. Hot, Cool, and Cold can be the account default and can be set per blob; Archive is only available per blob, not as an account-level default. Cool and Cold cost less to store but more to access, with lower availability SLAs.
flashcards.detail: Archive blobs are offline and must be rehydrated before they can be read, which can take hours. Cold, unlike Archive, can still be read immediately.

flashcards.front: Storage durability and recovery point objective
flashcards.back: Azure Storage always keeps three copies in the primary region. LRS offers at least 11 nines of durability, ZRS at least 12, and GRS and GZRS at least 16. GRS copies synchronously three times in the primary region and then asynchronously to a secondary region; GZRS uses ZRS in the primary and LRS in the secondary.
flashcards.detail: Because replication to the secondary is asynchronous, recent writes can be lost if the primary is unrecoverable. The typical gap, the recovery point objective, is under 15 minutes, but there is no SLA on replication time.

flashcards.front: Azure Data Box capacity and use
flashcards.back: A physical migration device shipped to you, with up to 80 TB of usable storage, for moving very large datasets when network transfer would be too slow. You order it in the Azure portal, fill it, and return it; imported data is uploaded to Azure and the device disks are wiped to NIST 800-88r1 standards.
flashcards.detail: It works for import and for export, including exporting large datasets from Azure for recovery or regulatory needs, and for one-time or periodic bulk uploads.

flashcards.front: Azure File Sync and cloud tiering
flashcards.back: Azure File Sync is installed on a Windows file server and keeps it bidirectionally synchronized with an Azure Files share. With cloud tiering, frequently used files are cached locally while rarely used files stay in the cloud until requested. Local access can use SMB, NFS, or FTPS, and a failed server can be replaced by installing it on a new one.
flashcards.detail: AzCopy sync only works in one direction, from a source you name to a destination. Storage Explorer is a GUI that uses AzCopy underneath.

flashcards.back: A managed domain service that provides domain join, group policy, LDAP, and Kerberos/NTLM authentication without you deploying or maintaining domain controllers. Azure runs two domain controllers, a replica set, in your chosen region, and information syncs one way from Microsoft Entra ID into the managed domain.
flashcards.detail: The classic answer for lifting a legacy app that needs LDAP or Kerberos into Azure. It is not Microsoft Entra Connect, which synchronizes an on-premises Active Directory with Microsoft Entra ID.

flashcards.front: Passwordless sign-in options in Microsoft Entra ID
flashcards.back: Microsoft Entra ID supports three passwordless options. Windows Hello for Business ties a biometric or PIN to a user's own Windows PC. The Microsoft Authenticator app turns a phone into a sign-in factor using number matching plus a biometric or PIN. FIDO2 security keys are phishing-resistant hardware devices, such as USB keys, that sign users in with no password.
flashcards.detail: Passwordless is not the same as MFA. MFA adds a second factor to a password; passwordless removes the password and relies on a trusted device plus a biometric or PIN.

flashcards.back: MFA asks for more than one kind of proof: something you know, such as a password; something you have, such as a code sent to a phone; and something you are, such as a fingerprint or face scan. A compromised password alone is then not enough to sign in.
flashcards.detail: Two items from the same category, such as a password and a security question, do not make MFA. Single sign-on is only as secure as the initial sign-in it relies on.

flashcards.front: B2B collaboration, B2B direct connect, and External ID for customers
flashcards.back: B2B collaboration lets external users sign in with their own identity to your apps, and they appear in your directory, typically as guests. B2B direct connect is a mutual, two-way trust with another Entra tenant that currently supports Teams shared channels; those users are not represented in your directory. Microsoft Entra External ID for customers, formerly Azure AD B2C, serves consumer and customer-facing apps.
flashcards.detail: The external identity provider handles authentication while you manage authorization to your applications. Access reviews help confirm guests still need access.

flashcards.back: A Microsoft Entra capability that asks guests themselves or a decision maker to recertify whether continued access is still needed, using suggestions from Entra ID, so access can be removed for people who no longer need it.
flashcards.detail: This is the answer for stale guest or permission sprawl: a recurring, reviewer-driven cleanup rather than a one-time policy.

flashcards.front: Defender for Cloud: secure score, benchmark, and just-in-time access
flashcards.back: Defender for Cloud builds on Azure Policy and aligns its recommendations with the Microsoft cloud security benchmark. It groups recommendations into security controls and calculates a secure score, raises security alerts with kill-chain correlation, and offers protections such as just-in-time VM access to reduce brute-force exposure.
flashcards.detail: Its three jobs are to continuously assess posture, secure by hardening to the benchmark, and defend by detecting threats. It covers Azure, on-premises through Azure Arc, and other clouds such as AWS and GCP.

flashcards.front: Azure RBAC inheritance and the allow model
flashcards.back: Role assignments are inherited: a role assigned at a management group, subscription, or resource group applies to everything beneath it. RBAC uses an allow model, so multiple assignments add up. It is enforced for actions that pass through Azure Resource Manager, not at the application or data level inside your own app.
flashcards.detail: Reader at a resource group plus Contributor at the same group gives the user Contributor-level permissions, not the intersection of the two.

flashcards.back: An AI assistant that gives administrators contextual, natural-language help: exploring services, understanding configuration options, and drafting commands or scripts. Some workflows can be agent-like and coordinate multi-step tasks.
flashcards.detail: Treat it as an operations assistant: validate its recommendations, confirm permissions, and review deployment changes before applying them. Azure Policy still enforces allowed locations, required tags, and approved SKUs on any change, however it was proposed.

flashcards.back: Both are command-line tools for managing Azure, available in Cloud Shell and installable on Windows, Linux, and macOS. They are functionally equivalent: Azure PowerShell runs PowerShell cmdlets while the Azure CLI uses Bash-style commands. Either can script repeatable, automated deployments.
flashcards.detail: Choosing between them mostly comes down to which syntax your team already knows.

flashcards.back: A web-based, unified console for building, managing, and monitoring everything from simple web apps to complex deployments, with custom dashboards and accessibility options. It has a presence in every Azure datacenter, so it survives individual datacenter failures, and it updates without downtime.
flashcards.detail: The portal is the graphical option; Cloud Shell, Azure CLI, and Azure PowerShell are the command-line alternatives, and all of them go through Azure Resource Manager.

flashcards.back: An initiative groups related policy definitions to track compliance with a larger goal, such as a regulatory standard. Policies and initiatives can be assigned at any scope and are inherited by everything beneath it, and built-in definitions cover areas like storage, networking, compute, and monitoring.
flashcards.detail: Policy can evaluate existing resources, block noncompliant new ones, and in some cases remediate automatically, for example adding a missing tag. Individual resources can be marked as exemptions.

flashcards.front: Cost alerts: budget, credit, and department quota
flashcards.back: Budget alerts fire when spending reaches a threshold you define. Credit alerts fire at 90 percent and 100 percent of an Azure Prepayment balance for Enterprise Agreement customers. Department spending quota alerts notify department owners when spending hits a set share of a quota, also for Enterprise Agreement customers.
flashcards.detail: A budget by itself only notifies; it can also be configured to trigger automation, such as shutting down nonproduction resources, but it does not block spending on its own.

flashcards.back: A Cost Management feature that visualizes spending so you can view total cost by billing cycle, region, resource, subscription, resource group, or service, and see accumulated cost over time against a budget.
flashcards.detail: Typical uses are spotting a sudden jump after a deployment, finding idle resources in nonproduction subscriptions, and checking that tags and budgets are working.

flashcards.front: Billing zones and data transfer costs
flashcards.back: Network traffic cost depends on geography. Some inbound data transfer is free, while outbound transfer is priced by billing zones, geographic groupings of regions used only for data-transfer pricing. Moving data within Europe costs less than moving it from Europe to Asia or South America.
flashcards.detail: Billing zones are not availability zones. One is a pricing grouping for bandwidth; the other is a set of physically separate datacenters inside a region.

flashcards.back: Arc projects non-Azure resources into Azure Resource Manager so they can be governed like native ones. Resource types hosted outside Azure include servers, Kubernetes clusters, Azure data services, SQL Server, and virtual machines (preview).
flashcards.detail: That lets Azure Policy, RBAC, and monitoring apply consistently across Azure, on-premises, and other clouds. Custom locations act as an abstraction layer over Arc-enabled Kubernetes clusters.

flashcards.back: ARM templates are declarative JSON that describe the desired end state. Azure validates the template, then deploys resources in dependency order and in parallel where possible. Templates are repeatable across environments, modular through nested templates, and extensible with deployment scripts.
flashcards.detail: Bicep expresses the same deployments in a simpler syntax and compiles to ARM templates. Both are infrastructure as code that can live in version control.

flashcards.back: A place to buy Azure-based solutions from third-party vendors, such as a preconfigured web server, a VM with specialized software, or a managed backup solution. Offers are certified and compliant with Azure policies and standards.
flashcards.detail: You may pay for the Azure services used plus the vendor's own services or expertise, and the billing structure is set by the vendor.

flashcards.front: Azure status vs. Service Health vs. Resource Health
flashcards.back: Azure status is a global view of Azure health across all services and regions. Service Health narrows to the services and regions you use, showing outages, planned maintenance, and health advisories, with alerts you can configure. Resource Health zooms in to one resource, such as a VM, and shows whether a problem is on Azure's side or yours.
flashcards.detail: Work from broad to narrow: widespread outage rumors, then your own services, then the single resource. Historical alerts are kept to help spot recurring trends.

flashcards.back: Synthetic requests that Application Insights sends to your application on a schedule so you know it is responding even during low-traffic periods. Application Insights is enabled by adding an SDK to the app or by enabling the agent without code changes.
flashcards.detail: Besides availability, it tracks request rates, response times, failure rates, dependency calls, page load times, user counts, and server performance counters.

flashcards.back: Purview has two main solution areas: risk and compliance, built on Microsoft 365 services to protect sensitive data and manage regulatory requirements, and unified data governance, which builds an up-to-date map of the data estate with automated discovery, sensitive-data classification, and end-to-end lineage across Azure, SQL and Hive databases, on-premises, SaaS, and other clouds such as Amazon S3.
flashcards.detail: Purview tells you what data you have and how sensitive it is; it is not the tool that grants or blocks access to it.

flashcards.back: A Microsoft portal with content, tools, and reports about Microsoft security, privacy, and compliance practices, such as audit reports and details of the controls that protect cloud services and customer data. My Library lets you pin documents and be notified when they are updated.
flashcards.detail: Some resources require signing in with a Microsoft Entra work or school account and accepting the Microsoft nondisclosure agreement for compliance materials.

questions.question: A startup wants to launch quickly with minimal infrastructure management, but portability to another cloud provider later matters more to them than convenience today. Which service model best serves that stated priority?
options: IaaS
PaaS
SaaS
A Reserved Instance commitment on a single VM family
questions.explanation: IaaS resources like VMs are the most portable between providers, since they're closer to raw infrastructure. PaaS launches faster but leans on provider-specific platform features that make leaving harder — a real trade-off, and the question asks which priority wins. A Reserved Instance is a pricing commitment, not a service model, and doesn't address portability at all.
questions.whyTested: AZ-900 likes stacking two competing priorities (speed today vs. portability later) in one scenario to see if you'll default to the 'easiest'-sounding answer instead of the one the question actually asked for — real projects make this exact trade-off, so exams probe whether you noticed which priority was stated as the deciding one.

questions.question: A finance team complains their monthly Azure bill is unpredictable and spikes randomly, even though nothing about their workload has changed. Which cloud characteristic is failing here?
options: High availability
Predictability
Scalability
Elasticity
questions.explanation: Predictability is about consistent, forecastable cost and performance — an erratic bill with unchanged usage signals this isn't being managed well. Scalability, availability, and elasticity all describe how resources respond to load, not billing consistency.

questions.question: An operations team manually adds two web servers the day before a product launch and removes them a week later. A colleague describes this as 'the app's elasticity at work.' Which term correctly describes what happened?
options: Scalability but not elasticity, because the change was planned and manual
Elasticity, because capacity both increased and later decreased again
Neither, because only automatic changes count as scaling at all
Elasticity for the scale-out step, and scalability for the later scale-in
questions.explanation: Scalability is the general ability to handle more load by adding resources, whether a human does it or not — which is exactly what this team did. Elasticity is the narrower, automatic form: capacity grows and shrinks in response to real-time demand without an administrator planning it. Growing and shrinking is not enough to make it elastic if each step was manual; manual changes still count as scaling; and the direction of the change (out versus in) has nothing to do with which term applies.

questions.question: A company currently spends heavily on capital equipment refreshes every three years for its datacenter. Moving fully to Azure IaaS would primarily shift this spending pattern to:
options: A one-time Reserved Instance prepayment classified as CapEx
OpEx
A smaller but still recurring CapEx
No change in spending pattern
questions.explanation: Cloud computing shifts organizations from large upfront capital purchases toward ongoing operating expense. Even an upfront Reserved Instance purchase is still billed as a discounted rate on consumption — it is still a consumption commitment billed through Azure, not an equipment purchase, so it is not CapEx — a commonly missed distinction.

questions.question: Which of these best illustrates the shared responsibility model shifting MORE responsibility to Microsoft, compared with a self-managed deployment?
options: Moving a file server to an Azure VM running the same OS as before
Assigning an additional RBAC role to the team managing a self-managed VM
Enabling a Read-only resource lock on a self-managed VM
Moving a database to Azure SQL Database (PaaS) instead of a self-managed SQL Server on a VM
questions.explanation: PaaS services like Azure SQL Database hand OS patching and infrastructure management to Microsoft, shifting more of the split toward the provider than a lift-and-shift VM does. A resource lock or an RBAC assignment changes who on your team can do what — it doesn't move any responsibility to Microsoft at all.

questions.question: A team wants to run a low-priority batch job at the lowest possible cost, and can tolerate the job being interrupted and restarted if Azure needs the capacity back. Which pricing approach fits?
options: Standard pay-as-you-go pricing
Reserved instances
Spot pricing
An Azure Savings Plan for compute
questions.explanation: Spot pricing offers deep discounts in exchange for the possibility of eviction with little notice — ideal for interruption-tolerant, low-priority work. Reserved instances and Savings Plans both trade a usage commitment for a discount, but neither involves eviction risk, so neither passes on the deepest possible discount this scenario allows for.

questions.question: A company uses Microsoft 365 for email, Azure App Service for its website, and SQL Server installed on an Azure virtual machine. A new hire claims the company 'uses no IaaS at all.' Which correction is accurate?
options: The SQL Server VM is IaaS; App Service is PaaS and Microsoft 365 is SaaS
App Service is IaaS, because the company deploys its own code to it
Microsoft 365 is IaaS, because it runs on infrastructure Microsoft owns
Both App Service and the VM are IaaS, since both host company workloads
questions.explanation: Installing SQL Server on a VM means the company manages the guest OS and everything above it — the defining trait of IaaS. App Service is PaaS: deploying your own code to a managed runtime is what PaaS is for, not a sign of IaaS. Microsoft 365 is a finished application the company only consumes (SaaS); the fact that it runs on Microsoft-owned hardware is true of every cloud model and doesn't make it IaaS. Hosting a workload isn't the test either — what matters is which layers the customer manages.

questions.question: A retailer's site traffic multiplies 10x during a single holiday weekend, then returns to normal a few days later. Which cloud characteristic most directly and cost-effectively addresses this, as opposed to simply over-provisioning fixed capacity year-round?
options: Zero Trust
Elasticity
Availability sets
Reserved Instances
questions.explanation: Elasticity lets resources scale up automatically for the surge and back down afterward, avoiding paying for peak capacity year-round. Availability sets protect against hardware failure, not demand spikes, and Reserved Instances lock in a fixed commitment — the opposite of what a short, unpredictable spike calls for.

questions.question: Why might an organization choose a hybrid cloud model even though it's more complex to manage than pure public cloud?
options: Hybrid deployments typically cost less overall than pure public cloud once egress and support fees are added in
Moving fully to public cloud removes the need to manage identity for any on-premises systems that remain
Regulatory or data residency requirements may require some data to stay on-premises
Azure's regional footprint covers most countries, which usually removes data residency as a reason to go hybrid
questions.explanation: Compliance and data residency needs are a common, legitimate reason to keep some workloads on-premises while using public cloud elsewhere — some regulations specifically require certain data to stay off public cloud infrastructure entirely, not just within a given country's borders. Hybrid isn't reliably cheaper once you factor in running two environments, and identity still has to be managed for whatever on-premises systems remain, typically unified with something like Microsoft Entra ID rather than eliminated.
questions.whyTested: This question isn't really testing whether you know what hybrid cloud is — it's testing whether you can spot a plausible-sounding but wrong justification for it, since three of the four options reference real IT concepts (cost, identity, regional coverage) just slightly misapplied. Exams pair a correct-but-unglamorous answer like compliance against tempting distractors to see if you're pattern-matching keywords instead of reasoning through the actual claim being made.

questions.question: A finance department wants to compare five years of projected on-premises costs against five years of projected Azure costs before deciding whether to migrate at all. Which tool fits?
options: Azure Advisor
The Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) calculator
The Azure Pricing calculator
Azure Cost Management
questions.explanation: The TCO calculator is built specifically to compare projected on-premises cost against projected Azure cost before a migration decision. The Pricing calculator estimates the cost of specific Azure resources you already plan to deploy, and Cost Management/Advisor both analyze spend on resources you already have running — none of the other three compare against an on-premises baseline.

questions.question: A CIO's migration business case lists four expected benefits of moving to Azure. Which one should be removed because it misstates how Azure works?
options: Capacity can be added in minutes without a hardware procurement cycle
Spreading a workload across availability zones can raise its availability
Microsoft takes over securing the company's data and user identities
Compute can automatically scale down during low-demand periods
questions.explanation: Under the shared responsibility model the customer always keeps responsibility for their own data, identities, and access, in every service model — so this line in the business case is simply wrong. The other three are genuine, well-documented benefits: agility (provisioning in minutes), high availability (zone-redundant deployment), and elasticity (automatic scale-down). Each of those is phrased with a hedge ('can'), which is exactly how a realistic benefit statement should read.
questions.whyTested: Rather than asking you to recite benefits, this puts one false claim among three true ones written in the same confident business-case voice. The trap is that 'Microsoft takes over security' sounds like a selling point until you remember the shared responsibility model never hands the customer's data and identities to the provider — an idea AZ-900 tests from several angles.

questions.question: A company wants to avoid vendor lock-in as much as possible while still gaining cloud cost savings. Which general guidance is most accurate?
options: Signing a Reserved Instance commitment is what creates vendor lock-in, not the service model chosen
IaaS workloads are generally easier to move between providers than deeply-integrated PaaS/SaaS workloads, though some lock-in risk always exists
Lock-in risk is the same across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS, since all three run on Microsoft-owned datacenters
Choosing PaaS over IaaS whenever possible minimizes lock-in, since PaaS abstracts away the underlying infrastructure
questions.explanation: IaaS resources are closer to raw infrastructure and generally port more easily than workloads built around a provider's specific PaaS or SaaS features. PaaS abstracting the infrastructure is exactly what deepens lock-in, not what reduces it, and lock-in risk very much differs by service model — a Reserved Instance is a pricing choice with no bearing on portability.
questions.whyTested: This question buries the actual concept, that IaaS ports more easily than PaaS, inside distractors that sound authoritative, like 'lock-in is the same across all models' or 'Reserved Instances create lock-in,' to test whether you can isolate the real driver of portability from plausible-sounding noise that name-drops adjacent AZ-900 concepts like pricing commitments.

questions.question: A company has Dev, Test, and Prod subscriptions and wants one policy requiring 'US regions only' applied consistently across all three, without configuring it three separate times or affecting other subscriptions outside this company's tenant. Where should it be assigned?
options: At the tenant root management group, since policy can only be scoped to an entire tenant
At each resource group individually, since policy cannot be assigned above the resource group level
Only through RBAC role assignments on each subscription
At a management group containing exactly these three subscriptions
questions.explanation: Management groups let you assign governance once and have it flow down to every subscription beneath them — creating one scoped to just these three subscriptions avoids configuring it three times AND avoids affecting anything outside that group. The tenant root group would work but is broader than needed; policy can absolutely be scoped above the resource group level; and RBAC controls permissions, not configuration rules like allowed regions.

questions.question: A team needs compute for a task that runs unpredictably, roughly twice a month, triggered by an uploaded file, and finishes in under 10 minutes each time. Which is the most cost-effective choice?
options: A single reserved-capacity VM instance
A VM Scale Set with a fixed minimum of 5 instances
Azure Functions (serverless)
A permanently running virtual machine
questions.explanation: Serverless Functions only bill for actual execution time, making them far more cost-effective than infrastructure that runs constantly for a task that fires a couple of times a month. A Scale Set with a fixed minimum still keeps 5 instances running at all times, and reserving capacity commits to paying for a VM whether or not the trigger ever fires.

questions.question: A company needs its on-premises network connected to Azure with predictable, low latency, avoiding the public internet entirely, for a latency-sensitive workload. Which service fits best?
options: VPN Gateway
A Virtual WAN hub connecting sites over the internet
Azure Front Door
ExpressRoute
questions.explanation: ExpressRoute provides a private, dedicated connection that doesn't traverse the public internet, giving the most predictable latency of the options here. VPN Gateway and an internet-based Virtual WAN hub both route over the public internet, and Front Door is a global entry point for web applications, not a site-to-site connectivity service.

questions.question: Two VMs host a stateful application whose instance count must stay at exactly two. The team wants protection from a single host or rack failure, and wants to avoid both VMs rebooting during the same planned maintenance, all within one datacenter. Which option fits?
options: Place both VMs in an availability set
Create a Virtual Machine Scale Set with autoscale rules
Put both VMs behind an Azure Load Balancer
Deploy the two VMs in two different regions
questions.explanation: An availability set spreads a fixed group of VMs across fault domains (separate racks, power, and switches) and update domains (separate maintenance windows) inside one datacenter — precisely the two protections asked for, with no change to instance count. A Scale Set is built to add and remove identical instances on demand, which conflicts with a fixed count of two stateful servers. A Load Balancer distributes traffic but has no say over where the VMs are physically placed. Two regions would protect against far more than a rack failure but adds latency and complexity the scenario never asked for.
