questions.question: A company keeps seven years of compliance archives that are almost never opened. If an auditor requests one, retrieval within a day is acceptable. Storage cost must be as low as possible. Which blob access tier fits?
options: Hot
Cool
Cold
Archive
questions.explanation: Archive has the lowest storage cost of all tiers, and its trade-off — data is offline and must be rehydrated, which can take hours — is acceptable when a day's retrieval window is fine. Cold is the nearest miss: it is also for rarely accessed data, but it stays online with millisecond access and costs more to store than Archive, so it isn't the lowest-cost choice here. Cool is for data accessed occasionally, and Hot is priced for frequent access — both would pay for responsiveness the scenario explicitly doesn't need.

questions.question: A company's backups must survive the loss of an entire Azure region. The budget owner asks whether zone-redundant storage (ZRS) alone meets that requirement, since it already keeps three copies. Which response is accurate?
options: No — ZRS keeps every copy inside one region; GRS or GZRS adds a copy in the paired region
Yes — the three ZRS copies are placed in zones that Azure spreads across separate regions
Yes — ZRS fails over automatically to the paired region during a regional outage
No — only LRS can be combined with a paired region for cross-region replication
questions.explanation: ZRS protects against a datacenter (zone) failure by spreading copies across availability zones, but all of those zones belong to the same region, so a regional outage takes every copy with it. Surviving that needs geo-redundancy — GRS or GZRS — which adds asynchronous replication to the paired region. Zones never span regions, ZRS has no cross-region failover to perform, and LRS is the least redundant option, not a prerequisite for geo-replication.
questions.whyTested: The exam likes to test whether 'three copies' sounds like enough to you. ZRS and GRS both keep multiple copies; the discriminating fact is how far apart those copies are, and the wrong options each offer a plausible-sounding mechanism (zones in separate regions, automatic failover) that would let ZRS do a job it cannot.

questions.question: A company wants every engineer to get their own isolated Azure environment for testing, with the company's security policies applied automatically without extra configuration per environment. Which combination enables this?
options: Separate subscriptions per engineer, grouped under a management group with policy assigned at that level
Separate resource groups per engineer within one subscription, with the same policy assigned individually to each resource group
One resource group shared by all engineers with individual RBAC roles
A separate management group per engineer, each containing its own single subscription with no shared parent
questions.explanation: Subscriptions give real isolation, and a management group above them lets policy apply automatically to every subscription beneath it — configured once, not per environment. Assigning policy to each resource group individually technically works but requires exactly the repeated configuration the scenario wants to avoid, and separate management groups with no shared parent would still mean setting the policy up once per engineer.

questions.question: Which identity feature lets a partner organization's employees sign into your app using their own company credentials, without you creating accounts for them in your directory?
options: Conditional Access
External identities
Azure RBAC
A dynamic security group
questions.explanation: External identities let outside users authenticate with their own existing identity rather than a new account in your directory. Conditional Access and RBAC both assume the user already has some identity in your system; a dynamic security group just auto-manages membership for accounts that already exist.

questions.question: A company wants to require MFA only when an employee signs in from a country they've never signed in from before, but not on every sign-in. Which feature enables this specific, condition-based rule?
options: Conditional Access
External identities
Enabling multifactor authentication for all users
Azure RBAC
questions.explanation: Conditional Access applies rules based on conditions like sign-in location, layering MFA on only when a condition is met. Enabling MFA for all users would require it on every sign-in regardless of location, which is more than this scenario asks for.

questions.question: A contractor signs in to the Azure portal from a compliant laptop but gets 'access denied' when restarting a VM. From an unmanaged tablet, the sign-in itself is blocked before the portal loads. Which pairing explains the two outcomes?
options: The restart failure is an Azure RBAC gap; the blocked tablet sign-in is Conditional Access
The restart failure is Conditional Access; the blocked tablet sign-in is an Azure RBAC gap
Both outcomes come from Conditional Access evaluating the device and the action
Both outcomes come from Azure RBAC, since role assignments can be scoped to a device
questions.explanation: The contractor could sign in from the laptop, so Conditional Access let them through; being unable to restart a VM once inside is a missing permission, which is RBAC's domain. Blocking the sign-in entirely from an unmanaged device is a device-compliance condition — classic Conditional Access, evaluated before any resource is touched. Conditional Access decides whether and how a sign-in happens; it does not grant or deny individual resource actions. RBAC assigns roles to identities at a scope such as a resource group, never to a device.
questions.whyTested: Rather than asking for definitions, this gives two symptoms and asks you to attribute each to the right control. The hinge is sequence: Conditional Access acts at sign-in, RBAC acts on resource operations afterward — the exam checks that you can place each tool at its stage rather than just knowing both names.

questions.question: A scenario describes an attacker compromising the network perimeter, but still being unable to access application data without passing separate identity and device checks. Which principle does this describe?
options: A perimeter-based security model
Zero Trust
Least-privilege access
Network segmentation with NSGs
questions.explanation: Zero Trust means never assuming trust based on network location — every request is verified on identity, device, and context, so breaching the perimeter alone grants nothing. A perimeter-based model is the opposite assumption: once inside, traffic is trusted, which is exactly what fails here. Least privilege limits how much an already-authenticated identity can do, but it isn't the principle that demands separate identity and device checks on each request. NSG segmentation filters network traffic by IP and port; it does not verify who or what device is making the request.

questions.question: A new administrator is asked to produce, with no setup work, a list of concrete changes to existing resources that would cut cost, improve resilience, and tighten security, based on Azure's own analysis of their configuration. Which tool should they open first?
options: Azure Monitor
Microsoft Defender for Cloud
Azure Advisor
An Azure Well-Architected Review assessment
questions.explanation: Advisor continuously analyzes your deployed resources and surfaces specific recommendations across cost, reliability, performance, security, and operational excellence — free and with nothing to configure. Defender for Cloud is the near-miss: it also recommends changes, but only for security posture, so it misses the cost and resilience asks. Monitor collects metrics and logs and raises alerts; it doesn't recommend configuration changes. A Well-Architected Review is a questionnaire-based self-assessment of a workload's design, not an automated scan of what is actually deployed.

questions.question: A company needs to move 200 TB of on-premises data into Azure Blob Storage, but their internet connection would take months to transfer it. Which service is designed for this scenario?
options: Azure File Sync
Azure Migrate
Azure Data Box
AzCopy over a site-to-site VPN
questions.explanation: Data Box is a physical device for transferring very large datasets offline when network transfer isn't practical. AzCopy over a VPN is still limited by the same slow internet connection — it doesn't solve the bottleneck, just moves it onto an encrypted tunnel.

questions.question: Which tool would an administrator use to script bulk, one-time file copies between an on-premises server and Azure Blob Storage from the command line?
options: Azure File Sync
AzCopy
Azure Migrate
Azure Storage Explorer
questions.explanation: AzCopy is the command-line tool built for scripted transfers. Storage Explorer offers similar transfer capability but through a GUI, not a script; File Sync is for ongoing, continuous synchronization rather than a one-time scripted copy; and Migrate is for assessing and moving whole workloads, not files.

questions.question: A company wants to manage on-premises servers and VMs in another cloud using the same Azure tools, like Azure Policy and RBAC, that they already use for native Azure resources. Which service enables this?
options: Azure Monitor
Azure Migrate
A hybrid Microsoft Entra Connect deployment
Azure Arc
questions.explanation: Azure Arc extends Azure management tooling — including Policy and RBAC — to resources outside Azure. Migrate assesses and moves workloads rather than managing them afterward, Monitor only collects telemetry, and Microsoft Entra Connect synchronizes identities, not resource governance.

questions.question: A company deploys VMs across two availability zones in the same region for resilience. Which failure scenario would this NOT protect against?
options: A single rack failing within one zone
A single datacenter losing power
A cooling failure in one zone's datacenter
The entire Azure region becoming unavailable
questions.explanation: Availability zones protect against datacenter-level failures within a region — power, cooling, or a single rack going down in one zone — because the other zone keeps running. They don't protect against a failure of the region itself, which needs geo-redundancy or a multi-region design.

questions.question: An application needs to authenticate a service, not a person, to access Azure resources without embedding a password in code. Which Entra ID feature fits?
options: A guest user account created for the application
Self-service password reset applied to a service account
A dynamic security group containing the application
A managed identity
questions.explanation: A managed identity lets an Azure resource authenticate to other services automatically, with Azure handling the credential entirely — nothing is embedded in code. The other three all still rely on a password or an account meant for a human, which is exactly what this scenario is trying to avoid.

questions.question: A company wants to prevent a storage account holding compliance data from ever being deleted, even by an administrator who has full Owner permissions on the subscription. Which feature should they apply?
options: A Delete resource lock
An Azure Policy with an Audit effect
Removing the Owner role from all administrators
A Read-only lock, since it is a stricter version of Delete
questions.explanation: A resource lock overrides normal RBAC permissions to prevent deletion, regardless of what a user's role otherwise allows — a Delete lock is exactly targeted at this requirement. Removing Owner roles is impractical and self-defeating; an Audit-effect policy only reports non-compliance without blocking anything; and a Read-only lock is stricter in a different way (it also blocks modification) but isn't 'more Delete' than a Delete lock.

questions.question: A company wants to both enforce a rule, like 'no VMs outside East US,' and separately get recommendations for improving cost efficiency of existing resources. Which combination is correct?
options: Azure Policy for both, since it can also generate cost recommendations
Azure Monitor for enforcement, Azure Policy for recommendations
Azure Advisor for both, since it can also enforce configuration rules
Azure Policy for enforcement, Azure Advisor for recommendations
questions.explanation: Policy enforces configuration rules going forward; Advisor analyzes existing resources and recommends improvements. Policy doesn't generate recommendations, and Advisor doesn't block or enforce anything — each tool does only one half of this scenario.

questions.question: A company needs to discover and classify sensitive data, like customer SSNs, scattered across multiple data stores in a hybrid environment. Which service is purpose-built for this?
options: Microsoft Defender for Cloud
Azure Policy, using a policy that audits storage account configurations
Azure Advisor, under its security recommendations
Microsoft Purview
questions.explanation: Purview is specifically for discovering, classifying, and protecting sensitive data, including across hybrid sources. Policy and Advisor both operate on resource configuration, not the content stored inside resources, and Defender for Cloud focuses on threat protection and security posture rather than data classification.

questions.question: An administrator wants to run Azure management commands from a browser on a locked-down machine where they cannot install software. Which tool fits?
options: The Azure mobile app
Azure Cloud Shell
Azure PowerShell
Azure CLI
questions.explanation: Cloud Shell runs entirely in the browser with nothing to install, unlike CLI or PowerShell, which are installed locally (though both are also available for use from within Cloud Shell). The Azure mobile app supports monitoring and basic actions, but not the same scripting/command experience.

questions.question: A team deploys environments with a long Azure CLI script that creates resources one by one. Re-running it after a partial failure errors out because some resources already exist. They want deployments that can be safely re-run and whose intended end state lives in source control. What should they adopt?
options: Declarative templates such as ARM or Bicep
A Read-only lock applied after each successful run
A longer CLI script with delete steps before each create
Azure Advisor operational-excellence recommendations
questions.explanation: ARM and Bicep templates are declarative: they describe the desired end state, and Resource Manager works out what to create, update, or leave alone, so re-running the same template is safe (idempotent) and the file itself is the version-controlled source of truth. The imperative CLI script is the near-miss — it can also be stored in source control, but it describes steps, not a state, which is why a re-run collides with what already exists. Adding delete-then-create steps makes re-runs destructive rather than safe. A Read-only lock protects what was deployed but doesn't make deployment repeatable, and Advisor can suggest improvements but never deploys anything.

questions.question: Which Azure tool would specifically flag that a company is paying for several unattached, unused disks?
options: Microsoft Purview
Azure Service Health
Azure Policy, if configured to deny disk creation
Azure Advisor
questions.explanation: Azure Advisor analyzes usage and cost, and will flag unused resources like orphaned disks as a cost-saving opportunity. A deny-effect Policy could stop new unattached disks from being created going forward, but it doesn't flag ones that already exist, and neither Purview nor Service Health looks at resource utilization at all.

questions.question: A company wants to know immediately if there's an ongoing Azure platform outage affecting a region they use, separate from the health of their own individual resources. Which service fits?
options: Microsoft Purview
Azure Service Health
Azure Monitor, using its resource health alerts
Azure Advisor
questions.explanation: Service Health reports on the health of the Azure platform itself. Azure Monitor's resource health signal is about your own resource's connectivity to the platform, not whether Azure's infrastructure in that region is having a broader outage — a subtle but real distinction.

questions.question: A web app in West Europe starts returning errors minutes after a deployment. Before rolling back, the on-call engineer wants to rule out a problem on Microsoft's side. Which tool answers whether the cause is a platform incident rather than their own release?
options: Azure Service Health
Azure Monitor metrics for the App Service
Azure Advisor reliability recommendations
Microsoft Defender for Cloud's secure score
questions.explanation: Service Health reports incidents, planned maintenance, and advisories affecting the Azure platform itself, filtered to the regions and services you use — the one place that says 'Microsoft has an active issue in West Europe.' Monitor metrics are the near-miss: they would confirm the error rate climbed, but they describe your resource's symptoms, not whether the platform underneath is at fault. Advisor offers longer-term design recommendations, not live incident status, and secure score measures security posture, which has nothing to do with an outage.

questions.question: A finance team wants monthly spending broken down by department, using labels applied to each resource when it was created. Which feature enables this, combined with Cost Management?
options: Management groups, since cost naturally rolls up by group
A separate subscription per department
Resource locks
Tags
questions.explanation: Tags are name/value pairs applied directly to a resource and used to filter cost reports by whatever label you choose, like department. A separate subscription per department would also let you break down cost, but it's a much heavier restructuring than 'labels applied to each resource' calls for, and management groups organize subscriptions for governance, not cost tagging.

questions.question: Which of these would Azure Policy be best suited to enforce?
options: Automatically scale a VM Scale Set based on CPU usage
Notify the security team when a login occurs from a new country
Every new storage account must use only approved SKUs
Give a specific user permission to restart VMs but nothing else
questions.explanation: The other three describe RBAC (a scoped permission grant), Conditional Access or an alert rule (a sign-in condition triggering a notification), and autoscaling respectively. Only the first is a standing configuration rule evaluated against resources — exactly what Azure Policy enforces.

questions.question: A production resource group carries a Delete lock. An administrator who is an Owner on the subscription must urgently delete one VM inside that group. Which sequence is correct?
options: Remove the lock, delete the VM, then re-apply the lock
Delete the VM directly, since Owner rights override the lock
Switch the lock to Read-only, which allows deletion but not edits
Wait for the lock to expire, since locks are time-limited
questions.explanation: Locks apply regardless of RBAC role — even an Owner cannot delete through one — and a lock on a resource group is inherited by every resource inside it, so the VM is covered. The only path is to remove (or temporarily remove) the lock, perform the deletion, and put it back; Owner or User Access Administrator rights are what allow managing the lock itself. A Read-only lock is stricter, not looser: it blocks modification and deletion. Locks never expire on their own.

questions.question: An architect wants one place to see health, performance, and log data across VMs, App Services, and databases, with the ability to configure alerts. Which service fits?
options: Azure Advisor
Azure Monitor
Azure Service Health
Microsoft Purview
questions.explanation: Azure Monitor is the unified telemetry, logging, and alerting service across your own resources. Service Health reports on the Azure platform rather than your workloads, Advisor gives point-in-time recommendations rather than ongoing telemetry, and Purview is focused on data governance, not resource health.

questions.question: Which Azure Monitor component would you use to write a custom query against collected log data to find failed login attempts in the last 24 hours?
options: Application Insights
Log Analytics
Azure Advisor
Azure Service Health
questions.explanation: Log Analytics is the querying and storage layer within Azure Monitor for exactly this kind of custom log query. Application Insights is scoped to application performance telemetry specifically, and Advisor/Service Health don't support custom log querying at all.

questions.question: A company is deploying identical infrastructure to Dev, Test, and Prod and wants a guarantee that all three are configured identically, with the deployment definition stored in source control. Which approach fits best?
options: An Azure Policy that audits each environment for drift after deployment
Infrastructure as Code using ARM templates
Azure Advisor recommendations
A single shared resource lock across all three
questions.explanation: IaC stored in source control is what guarantees identical, repeatable, trackable deployments across environments in the first place. An auditing policy could catch drift after the fact, but only once it's already happened — it doesn't guarantee the initial deployments matched, which is what this scenario asks for.

questions.question: An Azure Policy blocks creation of any VM without a 'CostCenter' tag, and a developer's deployment fails as a result. What does this indicate about the policy's effect setting?
options: It's using an Append effect, which adds the missing tag automatically
Policy cannot block deployments, only report on them
It's using an Audit-only effect, which only reports non-compliance
It's using a Deny effect
questions.explanation: A Deny effect actively blocks non-compliant deployments — the deployment failing is the tell. Audit only reports non-compliance without stopping it, and Append would add the missing tag automatically rather than blocking the deployment outright, so neither matches what happened here.

questions.question: A manager asks two questions: 'Exactly how much did the analytics team spend last month, by resource?' and 'Which of their VMs are oversized for their actual load?' Which tool answers each?
options: Cost Management cost analysis for the spend; Azure Advisor for the oversized VMs
Azure Advisor for the spend; Cost Management cost analysis for the oversized VMs
The Pricing calculator for the spend; Cost Management cost analysis for the oversized VMs
Cost Management cost analysis for both, since it includes right-sizing recommendations
questions.explanation: Cost analysis in Cost Management is the reporting tool for actual, historical spend, sliced by resource, tag, or time. Advisor is the tool that looks at utilization and recommends specific actions such as downsizing an underused VM. Swapping them fails because Advisor doesn't itemize invoices and cost analysis doesn't judge whether a VM is oversized. The Pricing calculator estimates the cost of resources you plan to deploy, not what you were actually billed, and cost analysis has no right-sizing logic of its own.

questions.question: In a PaaS deployment such as Azure SQL Database, responsibility for classifying the data and deciding who may access it transfers to Microsoft.
questions.explanation: Moving to PaaS hands Microsoft the operating system, database engine patching, and the underlying infrastructure — but data classification, identities, and access decisions stay with the customer in every service model, including SaaS. The misconception this statement encodes is that 'more managed' eventually means 'Microsoft owns the data responsibility'; the shared responsibility model never reaches that point.

questions.question: A virtual machine that has been stopped (deallocated) from the Azure portal continues to accrue compute charges until it is deleted.
questions.explanation: Under the consumption-based model, a deallocated VM releases its compute capacity and stops incurring compute charges; only its disks and any reserved public IP keep billing. The trap is the difference between stopping from the portal (deallocated, not billed for compute) and shutting down from inside the guest OS (still allocated, still billed) — the exam expects you to know that 'stopped' alone does not guarantee savings.

questions.question: In a PaaS service such as Azure App Service, the customer chooses when security patches are applied to the underlying guest operating system.
questions.explanation: Giving up control of the OS is the defining trade of PaaS: Microsoft patches the operating system and runtime on its own schedule, and in exchange the customer manages only the application and its data. A team that needs to control patch timing — for example to satisfy an audit window — needs IaaS, where the guest OS is theirs to patch. The statement describes IaaS-level control and misattributes it to PaaS.

questions.question: An Azure Functions app on the Consumption plan incurs compute charges continuously while it is deployed, even during hours in which no executions occur.
questions.explanation: Serverless billing is tied to execution: on the Consumption plan you pay per execution and for the compute consumed while code runs, and a function that is deployed but idle costs nothing in compute (its storage account still bills a small amount). This is what distinguishes serverless from a VM or an always-on App Service plan, which bill for provisioned capacity whether or not it is used. The statement applies the provisioned-capacity model to serverless, which is exactly the misconception the exam checks.

questions.question: Manually resizing a virtual machine from a D2 to a D4 size the night before a planned product launch is an example of elasticity.
questions.explanation: This is vertical scaling performed by hand — a legitimate example of scalability, since capacity was added to handle more load. Elasticity specifically means capacity expands and contracts automatically in response to real-time demand, with no administrator scheduling the change. A planned, manual resize fails the 'automatic' test, so calling it elasticity is the error the exam is probing for.

questions.question: Lifting-and-shifting on-premises servers to equivalently sized Azure VMs that run 24 hours a day captures the cloud's cost advantage on its own, because the billing is consumption-based.
questions.explanation: Consumption-based billing only saves money when consumption actually drops — by deallocating idle VMs, right-sizing, autoscaling, or moving to PaaS or serverless where appropriate. A like-for-like migration of always-on, fixed-size VMs reproduces the on-premises usage pattern in the cloud and can easily cost more than the hardware it replaced. The misconception here is treating pay-as-you-go as a discount in itself rather than an opportunity that still has to be exploited.

questions.question: Setting a Spot virtual machine's maximum price equal to the regular pay-as-you-go rate guarantees that Azure will never evict it.
questions.explanation: A Spot VM can be evicted for two reasons: the Spot price rising above your maximum, or Azure needing the capacity back. Setting the maximum price to the pay-as-you-go rate removes the first reason but not the second — a capacity-driven eviction can still happen with little notice at any price. That is why Spot is only suitable for interruption-tolerant work regardless of how the price cap is set, which is the point this statement gets wrong.

questions.question: If the region chosen for a resource group suffers an outage, the resources in that group that were deployed to other regions stop running as well.
questions.explanation: A resource group's region only determines where the group's metadata is stored. The resources inside can live in any region, and they keep running on their own regional infrastructure regardless of what happens to the metadata region — at most, management operations on the group could be affected while it is unreachable. The statement treats the group as a runtime boundary when it is only a logical management container.

questions.question: Deleting a resource group removes every resource it contains, and deleting a management group likewise removes the subscriptions beneath it.
questions.explanation: The first half is true and the second half is the trap. A resource group owns the lifecycle of its resources, so deleting it deletes everything inside. A management group is only an organizational container for subscriptions: it must be empty before it can be deleted, and moving subscriptions out of it (back to the tenant root group or elsewhere) leaves them intact. The exam likes to test that the two containers behave differently on deletion.

questions.question: Placing two virtual machines in the same availability set guarantees that they run in different availability zones.
questions.explanation: An availability set spreads VMs across fault domains and update domains — separate racks and separate maintenance windows — within a single datacenter. It says nothing about zones; both VMs can be, and normally are, in the same zone. Protection from a whole datacenter failing requires explicitly deploying the VMs into different availability zones, which is a separate choice (and the two options are mutually exclusive for a given VM). Confusing the two is one of the most common AZ-900 errors.

questions.question: A company that must encrypt its ExpressRoute traffic in transit has to configure that encryption itself — for example with IPsec or MACsec — because the circuit does not encrypt traffic by default.
questions.explanation: ExpressRoute's security comes from being a private, dedicated path that never touches the public internet, not from encryption. If a compliance rule requires encryption in transit, the customer adds it — a site-to-site VPN over the ExpressRoute private peering, or MACsec on ExpressRoute Direct. The contrast is VPN Gateway, which is encrypted (IPsec) precisely because it crosses the internet. Assuming 'private' means 'encrypted' is the mistake this statement is written to catch.

questions.question: An application using a storage account configured with geo-redundant storage (GRS) can read from the secondary region at any time, even before a failover is initiated.
questions.explanation: Plain GRS replicates data to the paired region, but that secondary copy is not accessible until a failover makes it the new primary. Read access to the secondary at any time is exactly what the read-access variants — RA-GRS and RA-GZRS — add, and that distinction is what you are paying for when you choose them. An app designed to serve reads from the secondary during a primary outage needs RA-GRS; with GRS it would simply fail until failover.

questions.question: Assigning an Azure Policy with a Deny effect automatically deletes existing resources that already violate the rule.
questions.explanation: Deny blocks new or updated deployments that would violate the rule. Resources that already exist are evaluated and reported as non-compliant on the policy's compliance dashboard, but Policy never deletes them. Bringing them into line is a separate remediation step — manual changes, or a remediation task for policies with DeployIfNotExists or Modify effects. The statement credits Policy with a destructive power it does not have, which is a frequent misconception.

questions.question: Adding a private endpoint to an Azure SQL Database automatically disables the database's public endpoint.
questions.explanation: A private endpoint adds a private IP for the service inside your VNet, so traffic from that network stays on the Microsoft backbone — but it is an addition, not a replacement. The public endpoint remains reachable until you separately turn off public network access (or restrict it with firewall rules). Teams that stop after creating the private endpoint have not actually reduced internet exposure, which is the gap this statement tests.

questions.question: A Conditional Access policy can require multifactor authentication from a user who holds no Azure RBAC role in any subscription.
questions.explanation: Conditional Access operates in Microsoft Entra ID at sign-in time and can be scoped to any user, group, or application — it has no dependency on Azure RBAC, which only governs what an identity can do with Azure resources after signing in. A user with zero Azure role assignments can still be required to pass MFA to reach Microsoft 365 or any other cloud app. Treating the two as linked, or assuming Conditional Access only matters for Azure administrators, is the misconception here.

questions.question: A subscription-level policy that denies resources outside East US can be overridden by assigning a more permissive allowed-locations policy at a resource group beneath it.
questions.explanation: Policy assignments accumulate down the hierarchy; they do not replace one another. A resource in that resource group is evaluated against both assignments, and the subscription-level Deny still blocks anything outside East US no matter what the lower-scope policy allows. A lower scope can only add restrictions, never loosen inherited ones — relaxing the rule for one group requires changing or exempting the higher assignment itself. The statement assumes 'closest scope wins,' which is how some systems work but not Azure Policy.

questions.question: A Delete lock applied to a resource group blocks deletion of the group itself but still allows individual resources inside it to be deleted.
questions.explanation: Locks are inherited by everything beneath the scope they are applied to, so a Delete lock on a resource group protects the group and every resource in it — the most restrictive lock in the chain applies. That inheritance is what makes a group-level lock useful for protecting a whole production workload with one setting. The statement imagines the lock as attached only to the container object, which would leave its contents unprotected; a Delete lock does still allow modification, but not deletion at any level.

questions.question: Azure Advisor can flag a single-instance virtual machine as a reliability risk, but it will not move that VM into an availability set or availability zone for you.
questions.explanation: Advisor is a recommendation engine: it analyzes configuration and usage and tells you what to change — a lone VM with no redundancy is a classic reliability finding — but it never alters resources. Acting on a finding is a separate step you take (or automate) yourself, which is also why Advisor recommendations tend to pile up unactioned in real subscriptions. The misconception on the other side would be expecting Advisor to remediate like a Policy remediation task or an Automation runbook; it does neither.

questions.question: Microsoft Defender for Cloud is the service you would use to scan an on-premises SQL Server and classify which columns contain credit-card numbers across a hybrid data estate.
questions.explanation: Discovering, scanning, and classifying sensitive data across hybrid and multi-cloud sources is Microsoft Purview's job — it builds a data map and applies classifications such as credit-card or national-ID patterns. Defender for Cloud is a security-posture and threat-protection tool: it can tell you a SQL server is misconfigured or under attack (and can reach on-premises servers through Azure Arc), but it is not the data-governance catalog that labels what each column contains. Both services touch 'security' and 'hybrid,' which is why the exam pairs them as distractors.

questions.question: Redeploying an unchanged ARM template to a resource group that already matches it creates a second copy of each resource.
questions.explanation: ARM templates are declarative and idempotent: Resource Manager compares the template's desired state with what exists and makes only the changes needed, so redeploying an unchanged template results in no changes rather than duplicates. That property is the whole reason templates are safer to re-run than an imperative script of create commands, which would collide with existing resources. The statement describes how a naive script behaves and misapplies it to IaC.

questions.question: Applying a CostCenter tag to a resource changes which subscription that resource's charges are billed to.
questions.explanation: Tags are metadata used to organize, filter, and report — in Cost Management you can group or filter spend by a tag such as CostCenter, which is exactly how chargeback reports are built. They never affect how a resource runs or where it is billed: charges always accrue to the subscription the resource lives in. Moving charges to a different subscription requires moving the resource itself. The statement confuses labeling spend for reporting with actually redirecting the invoice.

questions.question: A team is listing which parts of its proposed Azure design will never require them to patch an operating system. Which two services in the design meet that bar? (Choose two.)
options: Azure SQL Database
SQL Server installed on an Azure virtual machine
Azure App Service
Azure Virtual Desktop session hosts
questions.explanation: Azure SQL Database and App Service are PaaS: Microsoft owns the operating system and runtime patching, and the team manages only data and code. SQL Server on a VM is the near-miss — it is the same database engine, but running on IaaS, so the guest OS (and the engine itself) are the customer's to patch. Azure Virtual Desktop is a managed service for the brokering and gateway layer, but its session hosts are VMs in the customer's subscription whose Windows OS the customer still patches.

questions.question: A CTO drafts five expected outcomes of moving a line-of-business app to Azure. Which two are realistic expectations? (Choose two.)
options: Extra capacity can be added within minutes rather than after a procurement cycle
Microsoft assumes responsibility for classifying and protecting the company's data
Deploying across availability zones can raise availability beyond a single datacenter
The monthly bill becomes fixed and predictable regardless of how much is used
The service SLA guarantees the app will experience zero downtime
questions.explanation: Agility (provisioning in minutes) and higher availability through zone-redundant deployment are genuine, documented benefits. The other three each encode a common misconception: data classification and protection stay with the customer under the shared responsibility model; consumption-based billing makes cost track usage, which is the opposite of fixed — predictability comes from managing it, not from the model itself; and an SLA is a commitment with service credits for missed targets, never a zero-downtime guarantee.

questions.question: A development VM is only used during office hours but currently costs the same every month. Which two actions would actually reduce its compute charges under Azure's consumption-based model? (Choose two.)
options: Deallocate the VM from the portal each evening and start it each morning
Shut the VM down from inside the guest operating system each evening
Resize it to a smaller VM size that still handles the daytime load
Apply a Delete lock so it cannot be removed accidentally
Add a CostCenter tag so the charge appears under the development team
questions.explanation: Compute is billed while a VM is allocated, so deallocating it (portal stop, auto-shutdown, or CLI) removes roughly two-thirds of the hours from the bill, and a smaller size lowers the hourly rate for the hours that remain. The near-miss is shutting down from inside the OS: the VM stops but stays allocated, so Azure keeps charging for the reserved compute. A Delete lock protects the resource and a tag changes how the charge is reported — neither reduces what is consumed.

questions.question: Which two resources are required to establish a site-to-site VPN connection between an on-premises network and Azure? (Choose two.)
options: Local Network Gateway
VPN Gateway
ExpressRoute
Azure Bastion
questions.explanation: A site-to-site VPN needs a VPN Gateway on the Azure side and a Local Network Gateway representing the on-premises side. ExpressRoute is a separate, non-VPN connection type, and Bastion is unrelated to site-to-site connectivity.

questions.question: All four of these are real Azure Storage redundancy options. Which two replicate data to a second, geographically separate region? (Choose two.)
options: Locally-redundant storage (LRS)
Geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS)
Zone-redundant storage (ZRS)
Geo-redundant storage (GRS)
questions.explanation: GRS and GZRS both add asynchronous replication to a secondary, paired region on top of their base redundancy. LRS keeps all copies in one datacenter, and ZRS spreads copies across zones within the same region — neither one leaves that region.

questions.question: A company is choosing between an availability set and availability zones for a two-VM application that must stay in one region. Which two statements should guide the decision? (Choose two.)
options: Zones protect against an entire datacenter failing; an availability set does not
An availability set spreads VMs across racks and maintenance windows inside one datacenter
Zones automatically replicate the VMs to the region's paired region
VMs must be placed in an availability set before they can be assigned to zones
questions.explanation: The hinge between the two features is the failure they protect against. An availability set spreads VMs across fault domains (racks) and update domains (maintenance windows) within a single datacenter, so it survives a rack or host failure. Availability zones put VMs in physically separate datacenters within the region, so they also survive one datacenter losing power or cooling. Zones never replicate anything to another region — that is a different design — and the two features are alternatives for a given VM, not a prerequisite chain.

questions.question: A team has two workloads: a legacy Windows application that needs a custom kernel driver, and a two-minute cleanup job that runs each night. Which two pairings match each workload to the most fitting compute service? (Choose two.)
options: Azure Virtual Machines for the legacy application
Azure Functions for the nightly cleanup job
Azure App Service for the legacy application
Azure Container Instances for the legacy application
questions.explanation: A custom kernel driver requires control of the operating system itself, which only a virtual machine (IaaS) provides. A short, scheduled job that runs for two minutes a day is the textbook serverless case: a timer-triggered Function bills only for those minutes and needs no server left running. App Service and Container Instances are the near-misses for the legacy app — both can host Windows workloads — but neither lets you install kernel-level drivers into a managed platform's OS, so they fail the stated requirement.

questions.question: A governance team wants to stop any new storage account from allowing anonymous public blob access, and separately wants a report of existing VMs missing an Owner tag without blocking anyone. Which two statements about using Azure Policy are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: A Deny effect blocks creation of new accounts that allow public access but does not change existing ones
An Audit effect marks untagged VMs as non-compliant without stopping deployments
An Audit effect adds the missing Owner tag to each VM automatically
A Deny effect removes public access from accounts that already allow it
questions.explanation: Deny is preventive: it rejects new or updated deployments that violate the rule, and existing violators are only reported as non-compliant. Audit is informational: it flags non-compliance on the compliance dashboard and never blocks or changes anything, which is what the team wants for the tag report. Adding a tag automatically is the Modify (or Append) effect, not Audit, and no effect retroactively reconfigures existing resources without a separate remediation task — so the two distractors each give an effect a power it does not have.

questions.question: A Read-only lock is applied to a production resource group. Which three of the following operations will fail while it is in place? (Choose three.)
options: Resizing a VM in the group
Viewing a VM's CPU metrics in the portal
Deleting a storage account in the group
Listing the resources the group contains
Creating a new VM in the group
questions.explanation: A Read-only lock is inherited by everything in the group and blocks any operation that would change state — resizing (an update), deleting, and creating all fail, regardless of the user's RBAC role. Read operations are unaffected, so viewing metrics and listing resources still work. A common mistake is to assume Read-only only blocks edits to existing resources; creating a new resource inside the locked scope is a write to that scope and is blocked just the same.

questions.question: A startup on the free Basic support plan, with no paid add-ons, wants to improve its environment without increasing spend. Which two capabilities are available to it at no additional charge? (Choose two.)
options: Personalized Azure Advisor recommendations across cost, security, reliability, operational excellence, and performance
Azure Service Health alerts for platform incidents affecting its regions
Microsoft Defender for Cloud's enhanced workload protection plans
A committed one-hour response time from Microsoft for a production outage
An Azure Data Box device for moving data into Azure
questions.explanation: Advisor and Service Health are included with every subscription at no cost — Advisor's recommendations and Service Health's incident alerts need nothing more than configuring them. The near-miss is Defender for Cloud: its foundational posture features are free, but the enhanced workload protection plans the option names are paid per resource. A committed response time for a production outage requires a paid support plan, since Basic covers only billing and subscription issues. Data Box is a physical appliance billed per order plus shipping.

questions.question: A company runs SQL Server on an Azure VM (IaaS) and also uses Azure SQL Database (PaaS). Which two responsibilities belong to the company in BOTH deployments? (Choose two.)
options: Classifying the data stored in each database
Managing the accounts and identities that may access each database
Patching the database engine
Physical security of the datacenter hardware
Patching the guest operating system
questions.explanation: Data classification and identity and access management never leave the customer, whatever the service model — that is the fixed core of the shared responsibility model. The other three split by model: engine and guest-OS patching are the customer's job on the IaaS VM but Microsoft's job for Azure SQL Database, so neither is shared across both deployments, and physical datacenter security is always Microsoft's. Picking 'patching' is the typical error: it is true for one of the two deployments, not both.

questions.question: An administrator plans several changes to the company's Azure hierarchy. Which two of the planned actions are actually possible? (Choose two.)
options: Assign the Reader role at a management group so it is inherited by every subscription beneath it
Move a subscription out of one management group and into another
Place a single resource group under two subscriptions so both can bill for it
Nest a management group underneath a subscription to subdivide it
questions.explanation: Role assignments and policies made at a management group flow down to all subscriptions, resource groups, and resources beneath it, and subscriptions can be moved between management groups as an organization changes. The hierarchy is strict in the other direction: a resource group belongs to exactly one subscription, and management groups sit only above subscriptions — you subdivide a subscription with resource groups, never with another management group.

questions.question: One developer needs to run a single container for a 20-minute batch job with no orchestration. Another team needs a set of HTTP microservices that scale to zero when idle, without managing a cluster. Which two pairings fit? (Choose two.)
options: Azure Container Instances for the 20-minute batch job
Azure Container Apps for the scale-to-zero microservices
Azure Kubernetes Service for the 20-minute batch job
Azure Container Instances for the scale-to-zero microservices
questions.explanation: Container Instances is the fastest way to run one container on demand and let it finish, with nothing to orchestrate — ideal for a short batch job. Container Apps is built for microservices: it hides the Kubernetes cluster, handles HTTP ingress, and scales each service down to zero replicas when idle. AKS could run the batch job but would mean standing up and paying for a whole cluster for one container. Container Instances can't satisfy the microservices need because it has no built-in autoscaling or scale-to-zero — each instance runs until stopped.

questions.question: A company has an ExpressRoute circuit to Azure and is reviewing its resiliency and security design. Which two statements are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: A site-to-site VPN Gateway can serve as a failover path if the ExpressRoute circuit goes down
Traffic on the circuit is not encrypted unless the company adds its own encryption
When the private circuit is congested, ExpressRoute traffic is automatically rerouted over the public internet
Having ExpressRoute removes the need for network security groups on the Azure virtual network
questions.explanation: ExpressRoute and a VPN Gateway can coexist, and a common design uses the VPN as a cheaper backup path for the dedicated circuit. ExpressRoute's isolation comes from being private, not from encryption, so sensitive traffic still needs IPsec or MACsec layered on. The circuit never falls back to the internet — that would defeat its purpose; congestion is handled by bandwidth choice and redundant circuits. And a private connection says nothing about what traffic is allowed between subnets, so NSGs are still the traffic-filtering control inside the VNet.

questions.question: A company's backup data must survive a regional outage, and its recovery application must be able to read that data from the secondary region during the outage without waiting for a failover. Which two statements are accurate for choosing a redundancy option? (Choose two.)
options: RA-GRS (or RA-GZRS) allows the application to read from the secondary region at any time
Plain GRS replicates to the paired region but the secondary cannot be read until a failover
ZRS satisfies the regional-outage requirement at a lower cost than GRS
LRS is sufficient because its three copies are kept on separate racks
questions.explanation: The requirement has two parts — survive a region loss, and read from the secondary before failover — and only the read-access geo options satisfy both. GRS gets the data to the paired region but keeps the secondary unreadable until failover, so it fails the second requirement. ZRS keeps every copy inside one region, so it fails the first, no matter how much cheaper it is. LRS's three copies on separate racks protect against hardware failure in one datacenter and nothing wider.

questions.question: A security team wants to block the finance app for sign-ins from non-compliant devices, and separately wants to give the finance team Contributor rights on their resource group. Which two statements are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: Conditional Access can block access to the finance app when the device is not marked compliant
Conditional Access cannot grant Contributor; that requires an Azure RBAC role assignment
Conditional Access evaluates only external guest users, so employees would be unaffected
Assigning the Contributor role can itself enforce multifactor authentication at sign-in
questions.explanation: Device compliance is one of the signals Conditional Access evaluates, and blocking a specific cloud app on that basis is a standard policy. Granting permissions on Azure resources is a different job entirely — only an RBAC role assignment at the resource-group scope gives Contributor rights. Conditional Access applies to any identity you scope it to, employees included, and an RBAC role carries no authentication requirements of its own; MFA is enforced by Conditional Access, not by the role.

questions.question: An operations team sees disk latency spike on one of its VMs and, at the same time, hears rumours of a Microsoft outage in that region. Which two statements correctly describe which tool answers which question? (Choose two.)
options: Azure Monitor metrics show the VM's own disk latency over time
Azure Service Health shows whether Microsoft has an active incident in that region
Azure Service Health shows per-VM disk latency so you can confirm the spike
Azure Monitor requires a paid plan before it collects any platform metrics
questions.explanation: The split is 'my resource' versus 'the platform.' Monitor collects metrics and logs from your own resources, so the VM's disk latency lives there. Service Health reports incidents, maintenance, and advisories about Azure itself, filtered to your regions and services, so it answers the outage question. Service Health never shows a resource's performance counters, and basic platform metrics in Monitor are collected automatically at no charge — costs only come in for log ingestion and retention beyond the free amounts.

questions.question: An Azure service's SLA guarantees 99.9% monthly uptime. Which statement correctly describes what that commitment actually means?
options: The SLA applies only during the customer's local business hours, since that's when usage is highest
Microsoft commits to that uptime target and issues service credits if it isn't met, but some downtime can still occur
The customer is entitled to a full refund of that month's invoice the first time any downtime occurs
A 99.9% target is close enough to continuous uptime that Microsoft doesn't track or credit brief outages
questions.explanation: An SLA is a measurable uptime commitment backed by service credits when missed — it is not a zero-downtime guarantee, and outages are tracked and credited according to the SLA terms regardless of how brief. The remedy is a partial, tiered credit rather than a full refund, and SLAs run continuously rather than only during business hours.

questions.question: A web app depends on a web tier with a 99.95% SLA and a database tier with a 99.9% SLA, both of which must be up simultaneously for the app to work. What is true about the overall (composite) SLA?
options: Composite SLA only applies to services deployed in the same Azure region
The composite SLA is fixed at exactly 99.9%, since that matches the lower component
The composite SLA is lower than either individual component's SLA, since both must be available at once
The composite SLA equals whichever individual SLA is higher
questions.explanation: When dependent services must both be up, you multiply their uptime probabilities (0.9995 x 0.999 ≈ 99.85%), which lands below either individual figure — a scenario dependent on more sequential components generally has a LOWER overall SLA than any one piece. Composite SLA is a general math concept, not scoped to a region, and it isn't simply the higher or the lower value alone.

questions.question: A startup on the free Basic Azure support plan needs a guaranteed fast response time from Microsoft when a production system goes down. What should they do?
options: Nothing — Basic support already includes a committed response time for production-down issues
Purchase a Reserved Instance, which automatically upgrades support to Unified
Ask Azure Advisor to escalate the issue on their behalf
Upgrade to a paid support plan, such as Standard or Unified, which add committed response-time SLAs
questions.explanation: Basic support is free and covers billing/subscription questions, but carries no response-time commitment for a production-down technical issue — that requires moving to a paid plan (Developer, Standard, Professional Direct, or Unified, the current name for what was formerly called Premier), where response-time commitments get faster at higher tiers. A Reserved Instance is a compute pricing commitment unrelated to support tier, and Advisor gives configuration recommendations, not support-ticket escalation.

questions.question: A company owns on-premises Windows Server licenses with active Software Assurance. It will run Windows Server VMs in Azure around the clock for years and wants to cut the bill specifically by not paying Microsoft a second time for Windows. Which option targets that part of the cost?
options: A three-year Reserved Instance
An Azure Savings Plan for compute
Azure Dev/Test pricing
Azure Hybrid Benefit
questions.explanation: Azure Hybrid Benefit applies eligible existing Windows Server or SQL Server licenses to Azure VMs, removing the Windows licensing component from the hourly rate. A Reserved Instance and a Savings Plan are the near-misses: both are excellent for steady 24/7 usage, but they discount the underlying compute rate, not the license, and can be stacked with Hybrid Benefit rather than replacing it. Dev/Test pricing also removes Windows license charges, but only for non-production workloads under a Visual Studio subscription, which this long-running production fleet is not.

questions.question: A company wants to allow inbound traffic only on port 443 to a subnet of web servers and block all other inbound ports, without deploying a separate firewall appliance. Which Azure feature fits?
options: VNet peering to a separate management subnet that already has the desired port rules
A network security group (NSG) with allow/deny rules on the subnet
A Read-only resource lock applied to the subnet to prevent configuration changes
Azure Policy with a Deny effect blocking noncompliant inbound rules
questions.explanation: A network security group filters inbound and outbound traffic by port, protocol, and IP at the subnet or NIC level — exactly this scenario. A resource lock only blocks delete/modify of the resource's own configuration, not live network packets; Azure Policy governs configuration compliance, not traffic filtering; and peering just connects two VNets without adding any port-level filtering of its own.

questions.question: A web app in one region needs incoming HTTPS requests sent to different backend pools by URL path (/images versus /api) and protected by a web application firewall. The entry point must sit inside the company's VNet with a private frontend IP. Which service fits?
options: Azure Front Door
Azure Traffic Manager
Azure Load Balancer
Azure Application Gateway
questions.explanation: Application Gateway is a regional Layer-7 load balancer: it routes by URL path or host header, offers an integrated WAF, and is deployed into a subnet of your VNet, so it can expose a private frontend. Front Door is the near-miss — it also does path routing and WAF — but it is a global edge service with a public frontend that cannot be placed inside a VNet. Traffic Manager is DNS-based and steers clients to endpoints without inspecting HTTP at all. Azure Load Balancer works at Layer 4 and has no concept of URL paths or a WAF.

questions.question: A platform team runs dozens of containerized microservices. It needs direct access to the Kubernetes API to install custom operators and a service mesh, and wants control over node pool sizes and the node operating system. Which service fits?
options: Azure Container Apps
Azure Container Instances
Azure App Service for Containers
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
questions.explanation: AKS is managed Kubernetes: Azure runs the control plane, but you still get the full Kubernetes API, choose node pool sizes and images, and can install operators or a mesh of your choice. Container Apps is the near-miss — it also runs microservices with scaling and is built on Kubernetes underneath — but it deliberately hides the cluster, so there is no Kubernetes API or node pool to manage. Container Instances runs individual containers with no orchestration at all, and App Service for Containers hosts a web app's container inside the App Service platform, not a cluster you control.

questions.question: An organization wants to stop running its own name servers and instead have Microsoft's global network answer public queries for contoso.com, including its MX records for mail. Which service should they use?
options: Azure Private DNS zones
Azure Traffic Manager
Azure Front Door
Azure DNS
questions.explanation: Azure DNS hosts public DNS zones — A, CNAME, MX, and the rest — on Microsoft's global anycast name servers, which is exactly 'answer public queries for our domain.' Private DNS zones are the near-miss: same record types, but they resolve only inside linked virtual networks and are invisible to the internet, so public mail routing would break. Traffic Manager is DNS-based, but it steers clients among endpoints you register; it isn't an authoritative host for a whole domain and can't serve MX records. Front Door is an application delivery and routing layer, not a DNS zone host.

questions.question: An organization intentionally runs some workloads in Azure and others in a different public cloud provider, specifically to avoid depending on one vendor and to use whichever provider's service is strongest for a given need. Which deployment model does this describe?
options: Private cloud
Multi-cloud
Hybrid cloud
A single Azure region deployment with availability zones
questions.explanation: Multi-cloud specifically means deliberately using more than one public cloud provider. Hybrid cloud instead combines on-premises/private infrastructure with public cloud — a different axis entirely. Private cloud is dedicated to a single organization, and availability zones are a within-region resilience feature, unrelated to which providers are in use.

questions.question: A feature in Public preview in Azure always carries the exact same SLA guarantee as a Generally Available (GA) feature.
questions.explanation: Preview features are commonly excluded from SLA guarantees and may still change before reaching General Availability — the full committed SLA applies once a feature is GA.

questions.question: A 1-year Reservation and Spot pricing both discount Azure compute, but only Spot pricing carries the risk of the VM being evicted.
questions.explanation: A Reservation discounts a committed, predictable usage pattern with no eviction risk. Spot pricing discounts precisely because Azure can reclaim that capacity with little notice — a different trade-off entirely, even though both lower the bill versus pay-as-you-go.

questions.question: Which two statements about Bicep are correct? (Choose two.)
options: Bicep can only define compute resources, not networking or storage
Bicep deployments run through the same underlying Azure Resource Manager as ARM templates
Bicep is a simpler, more concise language that compiles down to ARM template JSON
Bicep replaces the need for Azure CLI and PowerShell entirely
questions.explanation: Bicep is a domain-specific language that transpiles to standard ARM JSON and deploys through the same Resource Manager engine as ARM templates — it's a friendlier authoring format, not a different deployment mechanism. It can define any Azure resource type, not just compute, and CLI/PowerShell are still used to trigger a Bicep deployment, not replaced by it.

questions.question: Which two statements accurately describe Microsoft's approach to helping customers meet compliance requirements in Azure? (Choose two.)
options: Achieving a certification like ISO 27001 for the Azure platform automatically certifies every customer's own workload built on it
Microsoft publishes independent audit reports and certifications, such as ISO 27001 and SOC 2, through resources like the Service Trust Portal
Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager gives a compliance score and recommended actions for your own environment
Compliance becomes entirely Microsoft's responsibility once data is stored in Azure
questions.explanation: Microsoft does publish independent audit reports/certifications and Compliance Manager does score and guide a customer's own compliance posture — but a platform-level certification doesn't automatically extend to a customer's own configuration and data, and compliance remains a shared responsibility, not Microsoft's alone.

questions.question: A startup wants to be able to spin up a new test environment in minutes rather than the weeks a traditional hardware procurement process would take, so they can experiment and iterate faster. Which cloud benefit does this best describe?
options: Agility
Elasticity
High availability
A composite SLA
questions.explanation: Agility describes the speed at which new resources can be provisioned and iterated on, cutting procurement time from weeks to minutes. Elasticity is specifically about automatically scaling existing resources up and down with real-time demand, not the initial speed of provisioning something new. High availability and composite SLA both describe uptime characteristics, not provisioning speed.

questions.question: A payment system is designed so that if one of its redundant application servers crashes, traffic fails over to a healthy server so fast that users notice zero interruption at all. Which term most precisely describes this specific quality?
options: High availability
Disaster recovery
Scalability
Fault tolerance
questions.explanation: Fault tolerance describes a system that keeps running with no perceptible interruption even when a component fails outright — the instant, seamless failover described here. High availability is the broader goal of staying up a very high percentage of the time, which can tolerate a brief blip during failover; fault tolerance is the stricter, zero-interruption version of that idea. Disaster recovery is the process of restoring service after a major outage has already happened, and scalability is about handling more load, not surviving a component failure.

questions.question: An application needs a NoSQL database that stays available with low-latency reads and writes across users on three different continents, automatically replicating data close to each region. Which Azure service is purpose-built for this?
options: Azure Table storage
Azure Cosmos DB
Azure SQL Database
Azure Queue storage
questions.explanation: Cosmos DB is a globally distributed, multi-model NoSQL database designed specifically for low-latency access across multiple regions, with data automatically replicated to wherever it is configured. Azure SQL Database is a relational, not NoSQL, PaaS database, and while it supports some geo-replication, it is not the multi-region, low-latency-by-design NoSQL service this scenario calls for. Table storage is a simpler NoSQL key-value store without Cosmos DB's global distribution features, and Queue storage is for messaging, not for serving application data reads at all.

questions.question: A development team wants to add image recognition to their app that can identify objects in a photo, without collecting training data or building and training their own model. Which Azure service fits best?
options: Azure Machine Learning
Azure Databricks
Foundry Tools (formerly Azure AI services)
Azure Synapse Analytics
questions.explanation: Foundry Tools (formerly Azure AI services, and before that Cognitive Services) provide pre-built, ready-to-call AI models, including image recognition, so a team can add this capability without training anything themselves. Azure Machine Learning is the opposite fit here — it is the platform for building, training, and deploying a custom model. Azure Databricks and Azure Synapse Analytics are both big-data analytics and processing platforms, not prebuilt AI capabilities.

questions.question: A manufacturer needs to securely connect and manage two million factory sensors, with reliable two-way communication between each device and the cloud. Which Azure service is designed for this?
options: Azure Logic Apps
Azure Event Grid
Azure Service Bus
Azure IoT Hub
questions.explanation: IoT Hub is purpose-built as a central message hub for secure, bi-directional communication between IoT devices and the cloud, and is designed to scale to large device fleets like this. Event Grid and Service Bus are both general-purpose messaging services, not designed specifically for device identity, provisioning, and device-to-cloud or cloud-to-device patterns at IoT scale, and Logic Apps is a workflow automation tool, not a device connectivity service.

questions.question: A large enterprise wants to negotiate a direct, multi-year agreement with Microsoft covering a committed volume of Azure and other Microsoft products, rather than paying by credit card as usage occurs. Which Azure offer type fits?
options: Pay-As-You-Go under a Microsoft Customer Agreement
An Enterprise Agreement (EA) / Microsoft Customer Agreement for enterprises
The Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) program
A Visual Studio subscription with monthly Azure credits
questions.explanation: An Enterprise Agreement (EA) — or its successor for enterprises, the Microsoft Customer Agreement for enterprises, as new EAs are being phased out — is a negotiated, direct, multi-year contract with Microsoft built around a committed volume of Azure and other Microsoft products, with centralized billing. Pay-As-You-Go under a Microsoft Customer Agreement is also a direct relationship, but it carries no upfront volume commitment and is billed as usage occurs — the model the enterprise is trying to move away from. CSP is the other near-miss: it is a real purchasing channel, but the agreement is with a Microsoft partner rather than negotiated directly with Microsoft. A Visual Studio subscription provides individual developer credits, not an organization-wide commercial agreement.

questions.question: Because Azure aggregates compute and storage demand across millions of customers in large-scale datacenters, it can typically achieve a lower per-unit infrastructure cost than most individual organizations running their own private datacenter.
questions.explanation: This is the economies-of-scale argument behind cloud pricing: pooling massive aggregate demand lets a provider buy hardware and power at a scale, and utilization rate, that a single organization's own datacenter usually cannot match, which is part of why cloud compute is often cheaper per unit than self-owned infrastructure of the same capacity. It doesn't mean cloud spending is automatically lower in every case — usage patterns still matter — but the underlying cost structure genuinely favors the aggregated, large-scale provider.

questions.question: An Azure Cost Management budget, once its spending threshold is crossed, automatically blocks any further resource deployment in that scope.
questions.explanation: A budget by itself only triggers an alert notification when its threshold is crossed — it does not automatically stop deployments or spending. Actually preventing further spend requires pairing that alert with a separate automated action, like an Azure Policy or an Automation runbook that reacts to the alert, which is not something a budget does on its own.

questions.question: A team wants databases where Microsoft patches the engine and operating system. It needs a relational T-SQL database for its ERP and a globally distributed NoSQL store for a mobile app. Which two choices meet both the management and the workload requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Azure SQL Database for the relational ERP workload
Azure Cosmos DB for the globally distributed NoSQL workload
SQL Server on an Azure virtual machine for the relational ERP workload
Azure Table Storage for the globally distributed NoSQL workload
questions.explanation: Azure SQL Database is fully managed relational T-SQL, and Cosmos DB is the managed NoSQL service designed for multi-region replication with low latency — both are PaaS, so Microsoft handles engine and OS patching. SQL Server on a VM meets the T-SQL need but fails the management requirement, because the team would patch the OS and engine itself. Table Storage is managed NoSQL, but it is a simple key-value store without Cosmos DB's turnkey global distribution, so it misses the workload requirement.

questions.question: A VM's monthly cost rose noticeably after a series of changes last month. Which two of those changes could explain the increase? (Choose two.)
options: It was redeployed from one region to another with higher per-hour rates
It stopped being deallocated overnight and now runs around the clock
It was renamed to follow the new naming convention
A Department tag was added for chargeback reporting
It was moved to a different resource group in the same region
questions.explanation: Region and consumption are two of the core factors that drive Azure cost: the same VM size is priced differently by region, and compute is billed for every hour the VM is allocated, so running 24/7 instead of office hours can roughly triple the compute charge. Names and tags are metadata with no effect on price, and a resource group is an organizational container — moving a VM between groups within the same region changes who manages it, not what it costs.

questions.question: On this real Create a resource group screen, Region is set to (US) Central US. Which statement about resources later placed in this group is accurate?
options: They may be in any region; Central US only stores the group's metadata
They must all be deployed to Central US
They can be in any region but are billed at Central US rates
They land in Central US unless the group is moved first
questions.explanation: A resource group is a logical container and management boundary, not a regional or billing boundary. The Region field on this screen decides where the group's metadata (its list of members and settings) is stored — a detail that matters for data-residency rules — but the resources inside can live in any region. Each resource is billed at the rates of its own region, not the group's, and there is no need to 'move' a group before placing a resource elsewhere.

questions.question: Using this real tab row from Create a storage account, an administrator must (1) allow access to the account only through a private endpoint and (2) enable soft delete for blobs. Which two tabs hold those settings? (Choose two.)
options: Advanced
Networking
Data protection
Encryption
Security
questions.explanation: The wizard splits concerns by tab. Networking is where you choose the connectivity method, including disabling public access and adding a private endpoint. Data protection is where recovery features live — blob soft delete, container soft delete, versioning, and point-in-time restore. Encryption is the near-miss many pick for 'security' asks, but it only covers encryption-at-rest keys. Advanced holds options such as the default access tier and hierarchical namespace, and Security covers account-level hardening such as secure-transfer requirements — neither one configures endpoints or soft delete.

questions.question: In this real Instance details section, Availability options reads 'No infrastructure redundancy required'. The team wants this VM and a second identical one to keep serving if one West US 3 datacenter loses power. Which change on this screen achieves that?
options: Availability options → Availability zone, one VM per zone
Availability options → Availability set containing both VMs
Security type → Confidential virtual machines for both VMs
Region → the paired region of West US 3 for both VMs
questions.explanation: Availability zones are physically separate datacenters within the region, each with independent power and cooling, so putting the two VMs in different zones is what survives one datacenter losing power. An availability set is the near-miss: it spreads VMs across racks (fault domains) inside a single datacenter, which protects against a rack or host failure but not the whole facility going dark. Security type controls features like vTPM and memory encryption, not placement. Switching Region would move both VMs together to a different region and still leave them in one datacenter there.

questions.question: In this real Access control (IAM) view of the example-group resource group, azure-user holds Contributor with the scope shown as 'Subscription (Inherited)'. Can azure-user delete a virtual machine inside example-group?
options: Yes — the inherited Contributor assignment applies to this group and its resources
No — inherited assignments grant read access only at child scopes
No — Contributor must be assigned directly on the resource group first
Only if azure-user also holds Owner on the resource group
questions.explanation: RBAC assignments flow down the hierarchy: a role granted at the subscription applies to every resource group and resource beneath it with its full permissions, which is exactly what the 'Subscription (Inherited)' scope column is telling you. Contributor can create, modify, and delete resources, so the VM can be deleted (unless a resource lock intervenes — nothing in this view suggests one). Inheritance does not weaken a role to read-only, no direct assignment at the group is needed, and Owner adds only the ability to manage access, which deletion doesn't require.

questions.question: A company moves its servers from its own building into a rented colocation facility but keeps buying and refreshing the hardware itself. The CFO says this completes the same CapEx-to-OpEx shift the cloud would deliver. Which assessment is accurate?
options: Facility costs become OpEx, but the hardware purchases remain CapEx
It is the full CapEx-to-OpEx shift, equivalent to moving to Azure
It is a move from OpEx to CapEx, since the lease is a long-term commitment
Nothing changes, because colocation is a form of private cloud
questions.explanation: Renting rack space turns the building and power into an ongoing operating expense, but every server refresh is still a large upfront capital purchase — the hardware is still owned. The cloud shift goes further because compute itself is consumed and billed as OpEx, with no equipment to buy. A lease is an OpEx commitment, not CapEx, so calling this a move from OpEx to CapEx has the direction backwards, and even if the arrangement were called a private cloud, the spending pattern has still partly changed, so 'nothing changes' is wrong too.

questions.question: A media company's video transcoding workload runs only when a customer uploads a new file, with uploads arriving at unpredictable times throughout the day. Which combination of characteristics would let them avoid paying for idle compute between uploads?
options: Elasticity combined with a consumption-based pricing model
High availability combined with a Reserved Instance commitment
Predictability combined with a fixed capacity reservation
Redundancy combined with a three-year Savings Plan
