questions.explanation: Elasticity lets compute scale down to nothing between uploads, and consumption-based pricing means they're billed only for compute actually used — together, no charge accrues while idle. A Reserved Instance or Savings Plan both commit to paying for capacity whether or not it's used, and neither high availability nor redundancy addresses idle-time cost at all.

questions.question: A regulated financial firm wants to modernize an aging application. They need to keep full control over OS-level security patching schedules for audit reasons, but also want Microsoft to manage the underlying physical hardware and virtualization layer. Which service model best fits, and why don't PaaS or SaaS work here?
options: IaaS, because PaaS and SaaS both hand OS patching to Microsoft, removing the firm's ability to control that schedule
PaaS, because it lets the firm choose its own patching schedule while Microsoft still manages hardware
SaaS, because it gives the firm the most granular control over the operating system
IaaS, because Microsoft delegates hardware management to the customer once they take on OS patching duties
questions.explanation: IaaS leaves OS-level patching in the customer's hands while Microsoft still manages the physical hardware and virtualization layer beneath it — matching both stated requirements. PaaS abstracts away OS management (the firm couldn't control its own patch schedule), SaaS gives essentially no infrastructure control at all, and the claim that Microsoft hands hardware management to the customer has the IaaS division backwards: Microsoft keeps managing the physical hardware in IaaS regardless of who patches the OS.

questions.question: A company deploys one VM in each of the three availability zones of East US. A manager concludes the app is now protected from an East US-wide outage because 'each zone is effectively its own region.' Which correction is accurate?
options: Zones are separate datacenters inside East US; surviving a regional outage needs a second region
The manager is right: Azure treats each zone as an independent region for failover purposes
Zones protect against regional outages only once GRS storage is attached to the VMs
Three zones automatically replicate the VMs to the East US paired region
questions.explanation: Availability zones are physically separate datacenters within one region, each with independent power, cooling, and networking. They protect against a datacenter failing, but an event that takes out the whole region takes every zone in it. Regional protection requires deploying to a second region (typically the paired region) and failing over to it. Zones are never treated as regions; GRS protects storage data, not running VMs; and nothing about using zones replicates VMs anywhere else.

questions.question: A company organizes its Azure resources so that a single resource group contains both a production web app in East US and its paired database in West US, deployed together for a coordinated app release. Is this a valid resource group design?
options: No, because a resource group can only contain resources from a single Azure region
Yes, because a resource group is a management boundary, not a regional one
No, because paired regions must be managed in strictly separate resource groups for compliance reasons
Yes, but only if both resources are deployed using the same ARM template
questions.explanation: A resource group is a logical container for managing related resources together (it is a management boundary, not a billing boundary) — it can hold resources from multiple regions, as this scenario does. It isn't restricted to one region, there's no rule requiring paired-region resources to sit in separate groups, and using a shared ARM template isn't a precondition for this being valid.

questions.question: A hospital network needs a connection from its on-premises datacenter to Azure that avoids the public internet for a latency-sensitive imaging workload, but the hospital's budget and timeline don't allow for the weeks-long circuit provisioning that a dedicated private connection usually requires. Which option best fits both constraints?
options: ExpressRoute, since it provides the most complete isolation from the public internet of any connectivity option
A site-to-site VPN Gateway, since it can be provisioned quickly and still encrypts traffic over the internet
Azure Bastion, since it provides secure remote access with very little provisioning delay
Azure Front Door, since it routes traffic through Microsoft's global network instead of the public internet
questions.explanation: A VPN Gateway can be stood up in hours over the existing internet connection, trading ExpressRoute's stronger internet isolation for something that actually fits this budget and timeline — the imaging workload still gets an encrypted, private-feeling tunnel. ExpressRoute better matches the latency/isolation goal in isolation, but its multi-week circuit provisioning is exactly what the scenario rules out. Bastion is for secure administrative access to VMs, not site-to-site connectivity between networks, and Front Door is a web-application entry point, not a private network connection.

questions.question: A finance team applied the tag CostCenter=Marketing to the Marketing resource group, yet cost analysis grouped by that tag still shows the group's VMs as untagged. What explains this?
options: Resources do not inherit tags from their resource group unless a policy or script applies them
Tags on a resource group apply only to resources created after the tag was added
Cost analysis can group by subscription tags, but not by resource-level tags
A Delete lock on the VMs is blocking the tag from propagating
questions.explanation: Tags are attached to the specific object they are placed on. Tagging a resource group tags the group itself; the VMs inside it keep whatever tags they individually carry, which here is none. To get consistent cost reporting you tag the resources themselves, typically enforced with an Azure Policy that inherits the group's tag onto new and existing resources. Creation time is irrelevant because inheritance isn't automatic in either direction; cost analysis groups by resource tags all the time; and a Delete lock only blocks deletion, not tagging.

questions.question: A team sets a monthly Azure budget of $5,000 in Cost Management and configures an alert at 80% of that budget. Partway through the month, actual spend reaches $4,200. What happens next?
options: Azure automatically stops all resources in the subscription once 80% of the budget is reached
An alert notification is sent, but resources keep running and spending is not blocked
The subscription is automatically downgraded to a free tier for the rest of the month
Azure Policy denies any further resource creation until the next billing cycle
questions.explanation: A Cost Management budget alert is purely a notification — it tells the team spend has crossed a threshold, but it doesn't stop resources, downgrade the subscription, or block new deployments on its own. Actually enforcing a spending cap would require a separate action, like an Azure Policy or an Automation runbook triggered off that alert.

questions.question: A security review produces two different lists of suggestions. One tool recommends resizing an oversized VM to cut cost, and separately flags a missing MFA requirement under its security recommendations. The other tool recommends enabling just-in-time VM access and patching a vulnerable container image, with no cost recommendations at all. Which tool produced which list?
options: The first list came from Azure Advisor; the second came from Microsoft Defender for Cloud
The first list came from Microsoft Defender for Cloud; the second came from Azure Advisor
Both lists came from Azure Advisor, which covers cost and security together in one place
Both lists came from Microsoft Defender for Cloud, which also gives cost-saving recommendations
questions.explanation: Advisor spans cost, reliability, performance, operational excellence, and security together — resizing for cost savings and an MFA gap are exactly the kind of two different pillars Advisor mixes into one recommendation list. Defender for Cloud is security-specific and wouldn't surface a cost recommendation at all — its list (just-in-time access, image vulnerabilities) has no cost content, which is the tell. The other two options either merge two genuinely separate tools into one, or hand Defender for Cloud a cost-recommendation role it doesn't have.

questions.question: A company runs several hundred VMs on VMware in a private datacenter whose lease ends in six months. The team wants to run those same VMware workloads in Azure without re-platforming each VM or retraining administrators. Which Azure offering is designed for this?
options: Azure Arc-enabled servers
Azure Virtual Desktop
Azure Data Box
Azure VMware Solution
questions.explanation: Azure VMware Solution lets an organization already established on VMware run those workloads in Azure with integration and scalability, which is the stated goal. Azure Arc-enabled servers is the near miss: it projects machines into Azure for governance and management but leaves them running where they are rather than moving them. Azure Virtual Desktop delivers desktops and apps, and Azure Data Box is a physical device for moving large amounts of data, not for running VMs.
questions.whyTested: Cloud models questions increasingly bring in a private cloud already built on VMware. The skill is separating a service that runs a workload in Azure from one that only manages it where it is.

questions.question: A VM running an in-memory database is running out of memory, and the team doubles the RAM by resizing the VM to a larger size. Meanwhile, a separate web tier is handled by adding six identical VMs behind a load balancer during peaks. Which pairing correctly names these two approaches?
options: The resize is horizontal scaling and the extra VMs are vertical scaling
The resize is vertical scaling and the extra VMs are horizontal scaling
Both are horizontal scaling because both add capacity
Both are vertical scaling because both involve virtual machines
questions.explanation: Vertical scaling changes the capability of an existing resource, such as adding RAM or CPU by moving to a bigger size, while horizontal scaling changes how many resources there are by adding or removing instances. The first pairing reverses the terms. Treating both as the same type ignores the difference the scenario is built around: one changes the size of a single machine, the other the number of machines.
questions.whyTested: Fundamentals exams like to give one workload two scaling stories and ask you to name each. Remember that up/down is size and out/in is count.

questions.question: Which statement about the Azure free account (free trial subscription) is accurate?
options: It includes credit to spend within the first 30 days, some products free for 12 months, and more than 25 always-free products
The included credit can be spent at any time during the first 12 months of the subscription
Every Azure service is free for the first 12 months, and the credit never expires
Usage beyond the free allowances is blocked until the owner explicitly chooses a paid plan
questions.explanation: The free subscription combines three things: credit to spend within the first 30 days, a set of products that are free for 12 months, and more than 25 products that are always free, subject to availability. It does not make every service free, and the credit does not stretch across the year. Usage beyond the free amounts is not simply blocked; it is charged at normal rates once the credit is gone or the free period ends.

questions.question: An architect documents geo-redundant storage for a Brazil South deployment and writes that Brazil South and its paired region back each other up within the same geography. Which correction is accurate?
options: Brazil South is paired in both directions with another region inside the Brazil geography, so the statement is correct
Brazil South has no pair at all, so geo-redundant storage is not available for deployments there
Brazil South is paired one way with South Central US, which is outside the Brazil geography, and South Central US is not paired back
Brazil South is paired in both directions with East US, which is outside its geography
questions.explanation: Brazil South is the documented exception: it is paired in only one direction with South Central US, a region outside its own geography, while South Central US is not paired back to Brazil South. Most pairs are bidirectional and within one geography, which is what makes this a trap. The claim that it has no pair is wrong because the pairing exists, and pairing with East US has no basis.
questions.whyTested: Region pair questions usually test the general rule and then probe the one famous exception. Knowing Brazil South is one-directional and cross-geography is a recurring detail.

questions.question: A team deploys to Poland Central, which has no traditional region pair. Their compliance lead asks how resiliency is typically provided there. Which answer matches Microsoft's description?
options: The region relies on availability zones and geo-redundant storage instead of a traditional pair
Such regions have no resiliency options available beyond a single datacenter
Customers must move to a sovereign region such as Azure Government to get redundancy
Microsoft automatically fails workloads over to the nearest paired region
questions.explanation: Regions without a traditional pair, including Italy North, Poland Central, and Israel Central, rely on availability zones and geo-redundant storage for resiliency. No pair also means no automatic failover to a partner region, and it does not mean resiliency is unavailable. Sovereign regions are a separate compliance concept and are not a way to add redundancy.

questions.question: A Chinese subsidiary must run on Azure regions that are physically and logically isolated from global Azure, in a model where Microsoft does not directly maintain the datacenters but works through a partner. Which option matches?
options: Azure Government regions, operated for U.S. agencies by screened U.S. personnel
An Azure availability zone inside a global Azure region
A region pair within the Asia Pacific geography, run by Microsoft directly
Microsoft Azure operated by 21Vianet (China East, China North)
questions.explanation: The China regions are available through a partnership between Microsoft and 21Vianet, so Microsoft does not directly maintain those datacenters, and they are a sovereign region. Azure Government is the near miss: it is also isolated but serves U.S. government agencies and partners and is operated by screened U.S. personnel. A region pair is a resiliency relationship and an availability zone is a location inside a region, so neither is an isolated cloud instance.

questions.question: Which of these Azure resources is described as zonal, meaning you pin it to a specific availability zone, rather than replicated across zones for you?
options: A zone-redundant storage account
A virtual machine
Azure DNS
Microsoft Entra ID
questions.explanation: VMs, managed disks, and IP addresses are zonal services: you choose the zone and any spreading across zones is your design. Zone-redundant storage is the opposite pattern, where the platform replicates across zones automatically. Azure DNS and Microsoft Entra ID are non-regional services that are always available from Azure geographies and resilient to zone-wide outages.
questions.whyTested: The three zone categories, zonal, zone-redundant, and non-regional, give exam writers an easy way to ask who is responsible for placement.

questions.question: A batch of CPU-intensive application tiers needs the best fit among VM families, while a separate dev/test box only needs occasional CPU spikes at low cost. Which pair of families matches these two needs?
options: N-series for the CPU-intensive tiers and M-series for the dev/test box
E-series for the CPU-intensive tiers and F-series for the dev/test box
B-series for the CPU-intensive tiers and E-series for the dev/test box
F-series for the CPU-intensive tiers and B-series for the dev/test box
questions.explanation: F-series is compute optimized, which suits CPU-intensive tiers, and B-series is burstable and cost-efficient, which suits dev/test workloads with occasional spikes. E-series is memory optimized, M-series is for very large memory footprints, and N-series is GPU-enabled, so the other pairings each assign a family to a job it is not built for.

questions.question: An administrator sees the VM size name D2s_v5 in a deployment template. Which reading of that name is correct?
options: D means disk optimized, 2 is the amount of RAM in GB, s means standard HDD, and v5 is the vCPU count
D means database workloads only, 2 is the number of data disks, s means spot pricing, and v5 is the Windows version
D means general purpose, 2 is the number of vCPUs, s indicates Premium SSD support, and v5 is the hardware generation
D is the datacenter, 2 is the zone, s is the subscription type, and v5 is the API version
questions.explanation: In VM naming, the letter is the family (D is general purpose), the number is the vCPU count, a lowercase s indicates Premium SSD support, and the version is the hardware generation. The other readings invent meanings: D is not disk, the number is not RAM or data disks, s is not HDD or spot pricing, and nothing in the name encodes datacenter or zone.

questions.question: A technician deletes a virtual machine from the Azure portal, yet the subscription's monthly cost drops by much less than expected. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Deleting a VM only pauses billing for the VM for one month before charges resume
Azure Policy adds a small charge for each deleted resource in a subscription
Reservations always keep billing the full VM price after a VM is deleted, whatever its size
The VM's disks, network interface, or public IP address were not deleted with it and still incur charges
questions.explanation: Provisioning a VM creates companion resources such as storage disks, a network interface, and often a public IP address, and removing the VM does not always remove them. Those leftovers can keep billing until they are cleaned up. Billing does not merely pause for a month, a reservation is a pricing commitment that is unrelated to deletion, and Azure Policy has no per-deletion charge.
questions.whyTested: Cost questions often hide a maintenance habit: deprovision everything a VM created, not just the VM.

questions.question: A support center runs three rotating shifts. Management wants every agent to get the same centrally managed Windows desktop, reachable from personal laptops and tablets, with data kept in Azure rather than on the devices. Which service fits best?
options: Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets
Azure Virtual Desktop
Azure App Service
Azure Bastion
questions.explanation: Azure Virtual Desktop delivers desktops and apps hosted in Azure to many device types, integrates with Microsoft Entra ID, and keeps data in Azure-hosted sessions. Scale Sets are groups of identical VMs for scaling applications, not a desktop delivery service. Bastion gives administrators secure RDP and SSH access to VMs, and App Service hosts web apps and APIs.

questions.question: A web application must run a script every night in the same context as the app, and the team wants to avoid managing any extra servers. Which App Service capability fits?
options: A private endpoint
An availability set
A VPN Gateway
WebJobs
questions.explanation: WebJobs run a program or script in the same context as a web, API, or mobile app, either on a schedule or on a trigger, and are commonly used for background tasks. An availability set groups VMs for resiliency, a VPN Gateway is a network connectivity service, and a private endpoint is a networking feature, so none of them runs scheduled code.

questions.question: A security team wants Azure SQL Database to be reachable through a private IP address taken from their own virtual network's address space. Which feature provides that?
options: A service endpoint
Virtual network peering
A private endpoint
A public IP address on the database server
questions.explanation: A private endpoint exists inside your virtual network and uses a private IP address from that network's address space, so the service is reached privately. A service endpoint is the near miss: it gives an optimized route on the Azure backbone and lets you restrict the service to chosen subnets, but it does not give the service a private IP in your address space. Peering connects two virtual networks, and a public IP is the opposite of what was asked.
questions.whyTested: Service endpoint versus private endpoint is a favorite trap because both sound like private connectivity. Look for the phrase naming a private IP address.

questions.question: A consultant working from hotels needs an encrypted connection from a laptop into an Azure virtual network, and there is no VPN hardware at any of the hotels. Which connection type fits?
options: Point-to-site VPN
Site-to-site VPN
ExpressRoute
Virtual network peering
questions.explanation: A point-to-site connection lets an individual client computer start an encrypted VPN connection into the virtual network, with no on-premises VPN device needed. Site-to-site links an on-premises VPN device or gateway to Azure, so it fits an office rather than a laptop. ExpressRoute needs a connectivity provider and a private circuit, and peering connects two virtual networks to each other.

questions.question: A company has ExpressRoute and states that none of its traffic to Microsoft ever crosses the public internet. Which fact shows that this claim is too strong?
options: ExpressRoute encrypts every packet with IPsec by default, so internet exposure is impossible
ExpressRoute connects only to Microsoft 365 and never reaches Azure compute or storage services
DNS queries, certificate revocation list checks, and Azure Content Delivery Network requests are still sent over the public internet
ExpressRoute traffic is always routed through the VPN Gateway before reaching Microsoft
questions.explanation: Even with ExpressRoute, DNS queries, certificate revocation list checks, and Azure CDN requests still use the public internet, so the claim overstates the isolation. ExpressRoute is a private connection and is not encrypted by default, so saying it encrypts everything is wrong. It connects to Azure services and also to Microsoft 365 and Dynamics 365, and it is not routed through VPN Gateway.

questions.question: A trading application stores many small objects in Blob Storage and needs very high transaction rates with consistently low latency. Which storage account type does Microsoft recommend for this?
options: Standard general-purpose v2
Premium block blobs
Premium file shares
Premium page blobs
questions.explanation: Premium block blobs are the premium type for block and append blobs, recommended for high transaction rates, smaller objects, and consistently low storage latency. Standard general-purpose v2 is the broad default but not the low-latency tier. Premium page blobs are for page blobs only, and premium file shares are for Azure Files rather than blob objects.

questions.question: Records must be kept at least 90 days, are rarely read, and must stay immediately readable with no rehydration wait. Which access tier gives the lowest storage cost that still meets these needs?
options: Hot
Cool
Archive
Cold
questions.explanation: Cold is optimized for data that is rarely accessed, stored at least 90 days, and still needs fast retrieval; it costs less to store than Cool and more to access. Archive is cheapest but is offline and needs rehydration, which breaks the immediate-read requirement. Cool is aimed at data kept at least 30 days and costs more to store than Cold, and Hot is the most expensive to store.
questions.whyTested: Newer tier questions use the Cold tier as the answer that sits between Cool and Archive.

questions.question: A company uses geo-redundant storage. The primary region is lost before the most recent writes finished replicating. What does the replication design predict?
options: Nothing is lost because GRS copies every write synchronously to the secondary region
Recent writes not yet copied to the secondary can be lost, and the gap is described by the recovery point objective
All data is lost because GRS keeps only a single copy of each object in one place
Only reads fail, because writes are always fully replicated before they are acknowledged
questions.explanation: GRS copies data synchronously three times in the primary region and then asynchronously to the secondary, so a failure can lose writes not yet replicated. The window is the recovery point objective, typically under 15 minutes although there is no SLA on replication time. Synchronous replication to the secondary is not how GRS works, a single copy is never kept, and writes are not guaranteed to be replicated before the failure.

questions.question: A branch office wants its local Windows file server to keep working as a cache: frequently used files stay on local disk, rarely used files live in Azure, and changes flow in both directions. Which solution fits?
options: Azure File Sync with cloud tiering
AzCopy sync run on a nightly schedule
Azure Data Box shipped to the branch office
Azure Storage Explorer installed on the server
questions.explanation: Azure File Sync keeps a Windows server bidirectionally synchronized with an Azure Files share, and cloud tiering keeps hot files local while rarely used files stay in the cloud until requested. AzCopy sync only copies in one direction between a source and destination you designate. Data Box is a one-time shipped device, and Storage Explorer is a GUI for managing storage rather than a continuous sync service.

questions.question: A company lifts a legacy application onto Azure VMs. It depends on LDAP binds, Kerberos or NTLM authentication, and Group Policy, and the team does not want to deploy or patch domain controllers. Users already exist in Microsoft Entra ID. What fits best?
options: Microsoft Entra Connect installed on the VMs
Microsoft Entra Domain Services
Azure RBAC with custom roles
A Conditional Access policy for the application
questions.explanation: Microsoft Entra Domain Services provides a managed domain with domain join, group policy, LDAP, and Kerberos/NTLM without you running domain controllers, and users sign in with their existing credentials. Entra Connect synchronizes an on-premises Active Directory with Entra ID, so it does not provide those domain services. RBAC controls what identities can do with Azure resources, and Conditional Access governs the conditions of sign-in.
questions.whyTested: Entra Domain Services versus Entra Connect is a classic naming trap. One is a managed domain; the other is a sync tool.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes how Microsoft Entra Domain Services receives identity information?
options: It synchronizes in both directions with Microsoft Entra ID, so objects created in the managed domain appear in Entra ID
It stores no user accounts, so every user and group has to be recreated by hand in the managed domain
It reads identities only from an on-premises Active Directory and never from Microsoft Entra ID at all
It performs one-way synchronization from Microsoft Entra ID into the managed domain, and resources created directly in the managed domain are not synchronized back
questions.explanation: A managed domain is configured for one-way synchronization from Microsoft Entra ID, and objects created directly in the managed domain do not flow back to Entra ID. In a hybrid setup, Entra Connect brings on-premises identities into Entra ID first, which then syncs to the managed domain. Two-way sync and manual recreation are both inaccurate, and it is not limited to on-premises Active Directory.

questions.question: Executives want to sign in by tapping a hardware key plugged into a USB port, with no password typed and strong resistance to phishing. Which passwordless method does this describe?
options: Windows Hello for Business
FIDO2 security key
Microsoft Authenticator number matching
A password plus an SMS code
questions.explanation: FIDO2 security keys are hardware devices, typically USB but also Bluetooth or NFC, that handle authentication without a username or password and are phishing-resistant. Windows Hello for Business ties credentials to a user's own Windows PC, and the Authenticator app uses a phone notification with number matching. A password plus an SMS code is multifactor authentication, not passwordless, because the password is still used.

questions.question: A project team invites supplier employees to a SharePoint site. The suppliers sign in with their own work credentials and show up in the company's directory as guest users. Which Microsoft Entra External ID capability is this?
options: B2B collaboration
B2B direct connect
Microsoft Entra External ID for customers
Microsoft Entra Domain Services
questions.explanation: B2B collaboration lets external users sign in with their preferred identity to your applications and represents them in your directory, typically as guest users. B2B direct connect is a mutual trust with another tenant that currently supports Teams shared channels, and those users are not represented in your directory. External ID for customers targets consumer-facing apps, and Domain Services is a managed domain service unrelated to guests.

questions.question: Guests from a finished project still have access to several resources. Security wants guest owners or managers to periodically confirm who still needs access, with access removed for those who do not. Which feature fits?
options: Resource locks
Azure Policy deny effect
Access reviews
Azure Advisor
questions.explanation: Access reviews ask guests or a decision maker to recertify continued access, and access can then be removed for people who no longer need it. Resource locks only prevent deleting or changing resources, Policy governs resource configuration rather than people, and Advisor offers configuration recommendations.

questions.question: An Owner role is assigned to a user at a management group that contains three subscriptions. A colleague says the role applies only to the management group object itself. What is accurate?
options: The role is inherited, so the user can manage everything in all three subscriptions beneath the management group
The role applies only if the same assignment is repeated separately on each subscription
The role applies only to resources that are created after the assignment was made
The role is inherited by the subscriptions but not by the resource groups beneath them
questions.explanation: Azure RBAC is hierarchical: access granted at a parent scope is inherited by all child scopes, so Owner at a management group covers every subscription, resource group, and resource beneath it. No repetition is needed, timing of resource creation does not matter, and inheritance continues all the way down rather than stopping at subscriptions.

questions.question: Which Defender for Cloud capability reduces exposure to brute-force attacks against VM management ports by keeping those ports closed until access is requested?
options: Azure Policy tag inheritance
A Delete resource lock
The Azure Advisor performance score
Just-in-time VM access
questions.explanation: Just-in-time VM access is one of the network protections Defender for Cloud offers to reduce brute-force exposure, opening management ports only when needed. A Delete lock stops resource deletion, an Advisor score is a recommendation metric, and tag inheritance is a cost-organization behavior; none of them controls port exposure.

questions.question: An administrator asks Copilot in Azure to draft an Azure CLI script that creates several storage accounts. Which approach matches Microsoft's guidance?
options: Run the script immediately, because Copilot output is already validated and exempt from Azure Policy checks
Treat Copilot as an assistant: validate the recommendations, confirm permissions, and review the changes before applying them
Skip RBAC checks entirely, because Copilot acts with its own elevated permissions in the subscription
Avoid Cloud Shell altogether, because Copilot replaces the command-line tools
questions.explanation: Copilot in Azure is an operational assistant, so you should still validate its suggestions, confirm permissions, and review deployment changes before applying them in production. Its output is not exempt from Azure Policy or from RBAC, and it does not replace Cloud Shell or the CLI.
questions.whyTested: Fundamentals content now includes responsible use of AI assistants in operations. The safe answer keeps a human review step.

questions.question: A platform team worries that AI-assisted deployments could create resources in regions the company has banned. Which control keeps enforcing that standard regardless of how a change was proposed?
options: Azure Service Health alerts for the affected regions
A cost budget alert at 80 percent of spend
An Azure Advisor reliability recommendation for each resource
An Azure Policy assignment that restricts allowed locations
questions.explanation: Azure Policy enforces standards such as allowed locations, required tags, and approved SKUs no matter whether a person, Copilot, or automation proposed the change. Service Health reports platform issues, Advisor only recommends, and a budget alert notifies about spending without blocking deployments.

questions.question: Which alert type notifies enterprise account owners when an Azure Prepayment balance reaches 90 percent and again at 100 percent?
options: Budget alerts
Department spending quota alerts
Credit alerts
Service Health alerts
questions.explanation: Credit alerts are generated automatically at 90 percent and 100 percent of the Azure credit balance for Prepayment, which is for Enterprise Agreement customers. Budget alerts fire on a threshold you set, department spending quota alerts relate to a department's fixed quota, and Service Health alerts are about platform events.

questions.question: A team wants nonproduction resources shut down automatically when a monthly budget threshold is crossed. Which statement about Cost Management budgets is correct?
options: Budgets are only available for Enterprise Agreement accounts and never for subscriptions
Budgets always stop all spending the moment the limit is reached, with no setup
Budgets can only send email notifications and cannot be connected to any automation at all
Budgets can be configured to trigger automation that suspends or modifies resources, in addition to sending notifications
questions.explanation: Budgets notify through budget alerts and can also be configured to trigger automation, such as shutting down nonproduction resources, when a threshold is reached. They do not stop spending on their own, they are not limited to email, and they are not restricted to Enterprise Agreement accounts.

questions.question: A company finds that moving 10 TB out of Azure from Europe to Asia costs more than moving it within Europe. Which concept best explains the pricing difference?
options: Availability zones inside each region
Billing zones used for data-transfer pricing
The management group hierarchy
Region pairs used for recovery
questions.explanation: Outbound data transfer is priced by billing zones, geographic groupings of regions used specifically for data-transfer pricing, so moving data across zones costs more than staying inside one. Availability zones are physically separate datacenters in a region, management groups organize subscriptions, and region pairs are a resiliency concept.

questions.question: A governance team wants to track compliance against a regulatory goal that involves dozens of individual rules. Which Azure Policy construct groups those related definitions?
options: A resource lock
A management group
A role assignment
A policy initiative
questions.explanation: An initiative groups related policy definitions so their combined compliance state can be tracked against a larger goal. A resource lock prevents deletion or modification, a management group organizes subscriptions, and a role assignment grants identities permissions, so none groups policy definitions.

questions.question: Before opening a support case, an engineer who is not signed in to any Azure account wants to know whether a widespread outage is affecting Azure as a whole. Which tool should they check?
options: Resource Health for a specific VM
Azure Advisor
Azure status
A Log Analytics query
questions.explanation: Azure status gives a global picture of Azure health across all services and regions and is the first place to look when a widespread outage is rumored. Resource Health describes one resource in your own subscription, Advisor gives configuration recommendations, and a Log Analytics query examines your own collected data rather than Azure-wide health.

questions.question: The same on-call group should be emailed and paged by a metric alert, a Service Health alert, and an Advisor alert. What is the efficient way to do this?
options: Create one reusable action group and reference it from all three
Create a separate action group for each alert and keep the lists in sync by hand
Use resource locks to route notifications
Tag each resource with the contact list
questions.explanation: An action group controls who is notified and what happens next, and action groups are reusable across Azure Monitor, Service Health, and Azure Advisor alerts. Maintaining duplicates by hand creates drift, and locks and tags do not route notifications.

questions.question: A low-traffic app is quiet at night, so nobody notices if it stops responding until morning. The team wants to know the moment it fails even with no real users. What should they configure?
options: A read-only lock on the app
An Azure Advisor cost recommendation
Application Insights availability tests
Reserved capacity for the app
questions.explanation: Availability tests send synthetic requests to the application so you learn it is down even during low-traffic periods. An Advisor cost recommendation is about spending, a read-only lock only prevents changes, and reserved capacity is a pricing commitment, so none of them detects an outage.

questions.question: A company buys a managed backup solution from Azure Marketplace. How is it billed?
options: Only the Azure services used are billed, and the vendor charges nothing beyond that usage
The Azure services used plus the vendor's charges, with the billing structure set by the vendor
A flat Microsoft fee that is set centrally by Azure Policy for all offers
The vendor's fee only, because the Azure resources behind a Marketplace offer are always free of charge
questions.explanation: Marketplace purchases may include the cost of the Azure services in use plus the vendor's own services or expertise, and the vendor sets the billing structure. Offers are certified to comply with Azure policies and standards, but that does not make the vendor's fee or the Azure usage free.

questions.question: In a SaaS deployment such as Microsoft 365, the customer remains responsible for the accounts and identities of its users and for the devices allowed to connect.
questions.explanation: Whatever the service type, the customer keeps responsibility for its data, the devices that connect, and the identities of people, services, and devices, while the provider always owns the physical datacenter, network, and hosts. SaaS shifts the most to the provider, but not these three.

questions.question: The credit included with an Azure free trial subscription can be spent at any point during its first 12 months.
questions.explanation: The credit must be spent within the first 30 days. The 12-month benefit applies to a specific set of products that are free for 12 months, alongside more than 25 products that are always free. Confusing the two periods is the common mistake.

questions.question: A storage account name may include uppercase letters and hyphens, as long as it is unique within its resource group.
questions.explanation: Storage account names must be 3 to 24 characters long, using lowercase letters and numbers only, and must be unique across all of Azure because the name forms the account's endpoint. Uppercase letters and hyphens are not allowed, and uniqueness within a resource group is not enough.

questions.question: Azure Data Box can only be used to import data into Azure; it cannot be used to export data out of Azure.
questions.explanation: A Data Box order can be an import or an export. Exporting large datasets from Azure for recovery or regulatory needs is a listed scenario, along with one-time bulk migration and periodic large uploads where online transfer is too slow.

questions.question: If one role assignment gives a user Reader on a resource group and another gives the same user Contributor on that group, the user ends up with only the more restrictive permissions.
questions.explanation: Azure RBAC uses an allow model, so assignments add up. The user has both the read permissions and the additional write permissions, which means Contributor-level access on that group. Restricting access takes a different mechanism, not a second, narrower role assignment.

questions.question: Azure CLI is limited to read-only operations, so creating resources requires Azure PowerShell.
questions.explanation: Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell are functionally equivalent; the main difference is syntax, with the CLI using Bash-style commands and PowerShell using cmdlets. Both can create, change, and delete resources and both are available in Cloud Shell and installable on Windows, Linux, and macOS.

questions.question: Every document on the Service Trust Portal can be downloaded anonymously, with no sign-in or agreement.
questions.explanation: To access some Service Trust Portal resources you must sign in with a Microsoft Entra work or school account and accept the Microsoft nondisclosure agreement for compliance materials.

questions.question: Which two actions are examples of vertical scaling? (Choose two.)
options: Resizing a database VM from 16 GB of RAM to 64 GB
Adding four identical VMs to a scale set before a sale
Moving a VM from a 2-vCPU size to an 8-vCPU size
Adding more containers to a deployment as traffic grows
questions.explanation: Vertical scaling changes the capability of an existing resource, such as adding RAM or CPU by moving to a bigger size. Adding VMs to a scale set or containers to a deployment changes the number of resources, which is horizontal scaling, specifically scaling out.

questions.question: Which two statements about security and governance benefits in the cloud are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: Templates help ensure deployed resources meet technical and regulatory standards, and can be updated at scale when standards change
Cloud-based auditing can flag resources that are out of compliance with a baseline and suggest mitigation
Moving to the cloud moves all OS patching to the provider in every service model
Because providers absorb DDoS attacks well, customers no longer need to manage user identities
questions.explanation: Templates and auditing are both governance benefits Microsoft describes. Patching is the near miss: on IaaS the customer still patches the guest OS, and only PaaS and SaaS shift most of that work to the provider. Identity management always stays with the customer, regardless of how well the provider handles network attacks.

questions.question: Which two statements about Azure VPN Gateway are correct? (Choose two.)
options: It is deployed in a dedicated subnet of the virtual network
A virtual network can have only one VPN gateway
A default deployment runs as a single instance with no standby
Traffic between sites travels unencrypted across the internet unless you add a separate encryption layer
questions.explanation: A VPN gateway is deployed in a dedicated subnet and only one can exist in each virtual network, although that one gateway can connect to multiple locations. By default it runs as two instances in an active/standby configuration, so a single instance is wrong. All data is encrypted inside a private tunnel as it crosses the internet.

questions.question: Which two statements about blob access tiers and scope are correct? (Choose two.)
options: Hot, Cool, and Cold can be set as the account default tier
The Archive tier can be set per blob but not as the account default
Archive can be set as the account default tier
Cool and Cold cost more to store than Hot
questions.explanation: Hot, Cool, and Cold can be set at the account level, while Archive is only available at the blob level. Cool and Cold have lower storage cost than Hot, with higher access costs, so claiming they cost more to store is backward.

questions.question: Which of the following are passwordless sign-in options supported by Microsoft Entra ID? (Select all that apply.)
options: Windows Hello for Business
Microsoft Authenticator sign-in with number matching and a biometric or PIN
FIDO2 security keys
A password followed by an SMS one-time code
questions.explanation: Windows Hello for Business, the Authenticator app, and FIDO2 security keys are the three passwordless options. A password followed by an SMS code is multifactor authentication, because the password is still part of the sign-in.

questions.question: Which two statements about Microsoft Defender for Cloud are correct? (Choose two.)
options: It groups recommendations into security controls and calculates a secure score
Its recommendations align with the Microsoft cloud security benchmark
It replaces Azure Policy, which is no longer used underneath it
It can assess only resources that run inside Azure
questions.explanation: Defender for Cloud groups recommendations into security controls, calculates a secure score, and aligns recommendations to the Microsoft cloud security benchmark. It builds on Azure Policy rather than replacing it, and it also covers on-premises resources through Azure Arc and other clouds such as AWS and GCP.

questions.question: Which two resource types can Azure Arc manage when they run outside Azure? (Choose two.)
options: Servers
Kubernetes clusters
Microsoft Entra tenants
Azure Policy definitions
questions.explanation: Arc projects servers, Kubernetes clusters, Azure data services, SQL Server, and virtual machines (preview) into Azure Resource Manager. A Microsoft Entra tenant is an identity directory and a policy definition is an Azure governance object, neither of which is infrastructure hosted outside Azure.

lessons.title: Cloud Fundamentals
lessons.summary: Service models, pricing, and the core benefits of cloud computing.
lessons.reading:
Cloud computing means renting computing power, storage, and services from a provider like Microsoft, instead of buying and running your own servers. You pay for what you use, which shifts spending from a big upfront purchase (CapEx) to an ongoing operating cost (OpEx) — similar to leasing equipment instead of buying it outright.

The three main service models — IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS — differ in how much you manage yourself versus how much Microsoft manages for you. IaaS is the closest to running your own servers: you get virtual machines and networking, but you're still responsible for the operating system and everything above it. PaaS removes that OS burden — you just deploy your code and Microsoft handles the runtime. SaaS is a finished product, like Microsoft 365, where you're just a user.

The shared responsibility model formalizes this: no matter which model you pick, you always keep responsibility for your own data and who has access to it.

Scaling comes in two directions. Vertical scaling changes the size of one resource, such as moving a VM to a size with more CPU and RAM, while horizontal scaling changes the number of resources, adding or removing VMs or containers. The cloud also changes the security and governance picture: templates and policies keep deployments aligned with standards, cloud-based auditing flags drift, and large providers are well placed to absorb distributed denial of service attacks. What never moves is the customer's responsibility for its data, the devices that connect, and the accounts and identities of people and services. Organizations with VMware already in a private cloud can run those workloads in Azure with Azure VMware Solution, and a new learner can try Azure with a free account that includes credit for the first 30 days plus a set of products that stay free for 12 months.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to cloud computing? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals:
If you've ever compared leasing a car to buying one outright, you already understand the CapEx-to-OpEx shift cloud computing represents. Buying a car, or a server, means a big upfront cost, but you own it forever. Leasing means smaller, ongoing payments and more flexibility to upgrade, but you never build equity in the hardware itself.

The service models follow a similar idea: IaaS is like leasing an empty apartment — you get walls and plumbing, but you furnish and maintain everything inside yourself. PaaS is like a furnished apartment — the basics are handled, you just move in and live. SaaS is like staying in a hotel — everything is handled for you, you're just using the room.
commonTraps: SaaS gives the LEAST control, not the most — IaaS gives the most control.
The shift is CapEx to OpEx, not 'free' — consumption-based pricing still costs money.
Elasticity is automatic scaling specifically; plain scalability can also be manual.
lessons.scenario: A small business currently owns three aging physical servers that need replacing every few years. Moving their line-of-business app to an Azure VM (IaaS) removes the hardware purchase entirely, shifting that cost to a monthly bill. If they later decide they don't want to manage patching either, moving that same app to App Service (PaaS) removes that burden too — at the cost of some control over the underlying environment.
lessons.onTheJob: In practice, the CapEx-to-OpEx pitch is what actually gets a cloud migration approved — finance teams often care more about moving a purchase off the balance sheet than about the technology itself. Expect "which service model" conversations to really be about who's on the hook when something breaks at 2am: IaaS means your team gets paged for OS patches and VM health, PaaS means Microsoft's SLA covers the runtime and your team only owns the app and its data.

lessons.title: Governance & Resource Structure
lessons.summary: Management groups, subscriptions, resource groups, and how policy flows through them.
lessons.reading:
Azure organizes everything you deploy into a hierarchy: management groups sit at the top, containing one or more subscriptions. Each subscription contains resource groups, and each resource group holds the actual resources — VMs, databases, storage accounts, and so on.

This hierarchy exists so you can manage things at scale instead of one resource at a time. A policy or access assignment applied at a management group automatically applies to every subscription, resource group, and resource beneath it. That's how a large company can enforce one security rule — like "only deploy to US regions" — across dozens of subscriptions without configuring it separately in each one.

Within this structure, Azure Policy enforces configuration rules, while resource locks protect individual resources from being accidentally deleted or changed, regardless of what a user's normal permissions would otherwise allow.

Below the hierarchy sit the physical building blocks. A region is one or more datacenters joined by a low-latency network, and a geography is a data residency boundary that holds regions. Availability zones are separate datacenters inside a region; services are either zonal (you pin them, like VMs and disks), zone-redundant (replicated for you, like zone-redundant storage), or non-regional (always available, like Microsoft Entra ID). Most regions are paired for recovery sequencing and staggered updates, but some, such as Italy North, Poland Central, and Israel Central, have no traditional pair, and Brazil South is paired one way with a region outside its geography. Sovereign regions, such as U.S. government regions and the China regions operated with 21Vianet, are isolated instances of Azure for compliance or legal needs. On the governance side, a policy initiative groups related policy definitions so you can track compliance against a larger goal, Microsoft Purview unifies data governance and risk and compliance, and the Service Trust Portal publishes Microsoft's audit and compliance documents.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to org-wide IT policy? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of this the way a company's org chart controls IT policy. If corporate IT sets a password policy at the company level, every department inherits it automatically — nobody has to configure it division by division. Azure's management group, subscription, resource group, resource hierarchy works the same way: rules set higher up flow down automatically, and you only have to set them once.
commonTraps: Deleting a management group does NOT delete the subscriptions inside it.
A policy at a lower scope can add restrictions, but never loosen what a higher scope already requires.
A resource group can hold resources from more than one Azure region.
lessons.scenario: An organization has Dev, Test, and Prod subscriptions, each needing the same "no deployments outside East US" rule and the same required tags. Rather than configuring that policy three separate times, an administrator creates a management group containing all three subscriptions and assigns the policy once at that level — it then applies automatically to every resource group and resource beneath it.
lessons.onTheJob: In practice, subscription boundaries end up drawn as much by billing and procurement as by security — splitting Dev, Test, and Prod into separate subscriptions is often driven by finance wanting a clean cost-center split as much as by any technical isolation need. Azure Policy assignments also tend to accumulate messily over time as different teams add their own rules, so a real governance review often turns up conflicting or redundant policies nobody remembers assigning, not the tidy single-policy story a training scenario describes.

lessons.title: Compute & Hosting
lessons.summary: VMs, containers, Functions, and how Azure keeps them resilient.
lessons.reading:
Azure gives you a spectrum of compute options, trading control for convenience. A virtual machine gives you a full OS you manage yourself — maximum control, maximum responsibility. Containers package an app with its dependencies, making it more portable and lighter-weight than a full VM. Azure Functions run small pieces of code on demand, with no server to manage at all — you're billed only for the time your code actually runs.

For resilience, Azure offers different tools depending on what you're protecting against: an availability set spreads VMs across separate hardware within one datacenter, so a single hardware failure or maintenance window doesn't take everything down at once. A VM Scale Set goes further, automatically adding or removing VM instances based on demand, so you're not paying for capacity you don't need.

Every VM is built from a size (cores and RAM), storage disks, and networking, and a few of those companions, such as disks, network interfaces, and public IPs, can outlive the VM and keep billing. Sizes are grouped into families: B-series is burstable, D-series general purpose, E-series memory optimized, F-series compute optimized, M-series very large memory, L-series storage optimized, and N-series GPU enabled, and in a name like D2s_v5 the letter is the family, the number the vCPUs, s means Premium SSD support, and v5 the hardware generation. When a team needs managed Windows desktops rather than servers, Azure Virtual Desktop hosts them in Azure, and App Service hosts web apps, API apps, mobile back ends, and WebJobs for background scripts.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to compute trade-offs? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: This is similar to choosing how much of a meal to cook yourself. A VM is like buying raw ingredients and cooking from scratch — total control over every detail, but you do all the work. A container is like a meal kit — the ingredients are pre-measured and prepped, you just do the final cooking. Azure Functions is like ordering delivery — you specify what you want, and it just appears, with none of the kitchen work on your end.
commonTraps: Availability sets protect against a single-datacenter failure, not a whole region.
Scale Sets add and remove instances automatically; availability sets are a fixed, static group.
Serverless means no server for you to manage — it's not just 'a smaller server.'
lessons.scenario: A nightly report-generation job runs for about 15 minutes once a day. Running it on a VM that stays on 24/7 would waste money on 23-plus idle hours daily. Running it as an Azure Function instead means paying only for those 15 minutes of actual execution — a direct payoff of matching the compute model to the workload's real usage pattern.
lessons.onTheJob: The VM-versus-container-versus-Functions choice in a real organization is driven less by architectural purity and more by what the team already knows how to operate and who gets paged if it breaks — a team with no serverless experience will often default to a familiar VM even when Functions would be cheaper, because the operational risk of the unfamiliar option outweighs the savings. Availability sets and Scale Sets are also the kind of thing that gets added to a postmortem after an avoidable outage, not configured up front, since the few extra dollars a month rarely feel urgent until something actually goes down. A subtler Scale Set misconfiguration shows up when autoscale rules trigger off average CPU across the whole set rather than per-instance load, which can hide one genuinely overloaded instance behind several idle ones while the average still looks healthy enough that scale-out never fires.

lessons.title: Networking
lessons.summary: VNets, subnets, and connecting Azure back to your own network.
lessons.reading:
An Azure Virtual Network, or VNet, is a private network you define in Azure, similar to a network you'd set up in an office. Subnets divide that VNet into smaller segments, similar to how VLANs divide a physical network by department or function.

To connect that VNet back to an on-premises network, Azure offers two main options. A VPN Gateway creates an encrypted tunnel over the public internet: cheaper and faster to set up, but subject to internet variability. ExpressRoute is a private, dedicated connection that doesn't touch the public internet at all, giving more predictable performance, though notably it isn't encrypted by default the way a VPN connection is.

VNets can also be peered together, letting resources in two separate VNets talk to each other directly — but that connection isn't transitive, so peering A to B and B to C doesn't automatically let A and C talk.

Beyond the basics, a service endpoint extends your virtual network to a service such as Storage or SQL over an optimized backbone route, while a private endpoint gives the service a private IP address inside your own address space and is the option Microsoft recommends for most new designs. VPN Gateway supports site-to-site, point-to-site, and network-to-network connections; it sits in a dedicated subnet, a virtual network can have only one, and by default it runs as an active/standby pair. Route tables, user-defined routes, and BGP steer traffic, network security groups and network virtual appliances filter it, and ExpressRoute Global Reach links your own sites over the Microsoft network, although DNS queries, certificate revocation checks, and CDN requests still cross the public internet.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to networking? See how this maps to a normal office network
lessons.fundamentals: If you've configured a small office network, this will feel familiar. A router directs traffic between different parts of your network — that's essentially what a VNet does automatically in Azure. VLANs that separate, say, guest Wi-Fi from the internal office network are conceptually the same idea as subnets separating parts of a VNet. And connecting two office locations with a site-to-site VPN is exactly the model VPN Gateway follows — just connecting to Azure instead of another physical office.
commonTraps: ExpressRoute is private, but NOT encrypted by default — VPN Gateway is the encrypted one.
VNet peering isn't transitive: A peered to B and B peered to C doesn't mean A and C can talk.
A private endpoint gets a private IP — it is not reachable from the internet.
lessons.scenario: A company's finance team sits in one subnet and its public-facing web servers in another, both inside the same VNet, with a rule blocking the finance subnet from being reached externally. When the company opens a second office, they connect it to Azure with a VPN Gateway rather than ExpressRoute, since the link doesn't need dedicated bandwidth — just a secure connection over their existing internet line.
lessons.onTheJob: ExpressRoute's real cost isn't just the Azure side of the bill — provisioning it involves a telecom carrier, a physical circuit, and often weeks of lead time, which is why most smaller organizations stick with VPN Gateway despite ExpressRoute's better latency profile on paper. Networking changes are also usually the most tightly change-controlled work in a production Azure environment, because a subnet or peering mistake can quietly take down connectivity for teams that had nothing to do with the change that caused it.

lessons.title: Storage
lessons.summary: Blob, Files, Queue, Table, access tiers, and redundancy.
lessons.reading:
Azure Storage accounts hold four main types of data (a fifth core service, Disk storage, supplies the managed disks that back VMs): Blob storage for unstructured files like images and backups, Azure Files for SMB or NFS file shares you can mount like a network drive, Queue storage for lightweight messaging between applications, and Table storage for simple key-value data.

Within Blob storage, access tiers let you balance cost against how quickly you need to retrieve data. Hot tier costs more to store but is fastest and cheapest to access — good for data you use constantly. Archive tier is the opposite: cheapest to store, but can take hours to retrieve — good for compliance data you rarely need to touch.

Redundancy options protect that data against hardware and datacenter failure. Locally-redundant storage keeps copies within one datacenter. Zone-redundant storage spreads copies across datacenters within a region. Geo-redundant storage goes further, copying to a second region entirely — essential if you need to survive a full regional outage.

Account type matters as well: standard general-purpose v2 is the default for most scenarios, while premium block blobs, premium file shares, and premium page blobs trade cost for low latency and high transaction rates and offer only LRS or ZRS (page blobs only LRS). The Cool, Cold, and Archive tiers carry minimum stays of 30, 90, and 180 days; Archive can only be set per blob and must be rehydrated before reading, while Cold stays online. Redundancy durability grows from 11 nines for LRS to 12 for ZRS and at least 16 for GRS and GZRS, but replication to the secondary region is asynchronous, so the recovery point objective, typically under 15 minutes, is still the data you could lose. To move data, Azure Data Box ships up to 80 TB of usable capacity for import or export, and Azure File Sync keeps a Windows server in two-way sync with Azure Files with cloud tiering, unlike AzCopy sync, which only copies one way.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to storage tiers? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: Think of storage tiers like a filing system: papers you use every day sit on your desk, the Hot tier, quick to grab, but desk space is expensive. Papers you rarely need go in a storage unit across town, the Archive tier, cheap to keep, but it takes real time to go get them. Redundancy is like keeping copies of important documents: one copy in your desk drawer is fine for a coffee spill, but if your whole office could burn down, you'd want a copy at a friend's house across town too.
commonTraps: Archive tier is cheapest to store but can take hours to retrieve — don't pick it for data you access often.
ZRS protects against a datacenter failure within a region, not a full region going down — that needs GRS.
Plain GRS isn't readable from the secondary region until failover — RA-GRS is the one you can read from directly.
lessons.scenario: A healthcare provider must keep patient records for seven years for compliance, but almost never opens files older than a year. Storing everything in Hot tier would be needlessly expensive. Moving records older than 12 months to Archive tier with a lifecycle management policy keeps them retrievable within the required window while cutting storage cost dramatically.
lessons.onTheJob: Lifecycle management policies that automatically move aging data to Cool or Archive tiers are one of the highest-leverage, easiest-to-forget cost levers in a real subscription — a team that never configures one is often quietly overpaying for years without anyone noticing on the monthly bill. Choosing a redundancy option is also genuinely a conversation between whoever owns the compliance requirement and whoever owns the budget, since GRS roughly doubles storage cost for protection that may never actually get used. A common misconception with GRS specifically is assuming failover to the secondary region happens automatically the moment the primary goes down — for most storage accounts a failover has to be explicitly triggered, so a disaster-recovery plan that never actually rehearses that trigger step hasn't really been tested at all.

lessons.title: Identity & Security
lessons.summary: Entra ID, RBAC, Conditional Access, and the Zero Trust mindset.
lessons.reading:
Microsoft Entra ID, formerly Azure Active Directory, is Azure's identity service — it manages users, groups, and what they're allowed to access. Two related but different tools control that access: Azure RBAC decides what an identity can do, like "this user can restart VMs," assigned at a scope such as a subscription or resource group. Conditional Access decides under what conditions someone is allowed to sign in at all — for example, requiring MFA only when someone signs in from an unfamiliar location or an unmanaged device.

Zero Trust is the security philosophy underlying a lot of this: never assume trust just because a request came from inside the network. Every request gets verified independently, based on identity, device, and context, regardless of where it's coming from. Defense-in-depth complements this with layered protection — physical, identity, network, and data layers — so that a single breach doesn't expose everything.

Microsoft Entra Domain Services provides a managed domain, with domain join, group policy, LDAP, and Kerberos/NTLM, so legacy apps can move to Azure without you running domain controllers; it syncs one way from Entra ID, unlike Entra Connect, which links an on-premises Active Directory to Entra ID. Passwordless sign-in comes in three forms: Windows Hello for Business, the Microsoft Authenticator app, and FIDO2 security keys. External users arrive through B2B collaboration (guests in your directory) or B2B direct connect (Teams shared channels), and access reviews prune guests who no longer need access. Azure RBAC assignments are inherited down the hierarchy and are additive, and Defender for Cloud turns recommendations aligned to the Microsoft cloud security benchmark into a secure score and offers just-in-time VM access.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to identity and access concepts? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: In a traditional office, security might mean a badge to get in the front door, plus a separate key for the server room, plus a password for the file server. Each layer is a separate checkpoint, and getting through one doesn't automatically get you through the next — that's defense-in-depth. Conditional Access is like a smart badge reader that also checks the time of day and whether it recognizes your device, not just whether you have a valid badge. RBAC is simpler: it's just the list of which doors your badge actually opens.
commonTraps: RBAC is what you can do. Conditional Access is under what conditions you can sign in at all — different jobs.
Zero Trust means never trusting a request just because it's inside the network perimeter.
MFA and passwordless aren't the same thing — passwordless doesn't use a password at all.
lessons.scenario: An IT team grants a support technician Contributor access to a single resource group, so they can restart VMs there but nowhere else. Separately, they set up a Conditional Access policy requiring MFA whenever anyone signs in from outside the corporate network. Together, RBAC controls what the technician can touch, and Conditional Access controls the circumstances under which they're allowed in at all.
lessons.onTheJob: RBAC assignments in a real tenant tend to sprawl into 'temporary' access grants that never get revoked, so periodic access reviews are less about clean exam-style role design and more about cleaning up permission debt nobody remembers creating. Conditional Access is also where a lot of real help-desk tickets originate — a policy tightened for good security reasons locks out a legitimate traveling employee, and someone has to weigh the security team's Zero Trust stance against a person just trying to do their job. This same Conditional Access mechanism carries straight into AZ-104, Azure Administrator, where the exam goes a level deeper and expects you to reason about it layering on top of RBAC scope and inheritance rather than replacing either one.

lessons.title: Cost, Policy & Monitoring
lessons.summary: Keeping an environment compliant, affordable, and healthy day to day.
lessons.reading:
Managing an Azure environment day to day means keeping an eye on cost, compliance, and health. Azure Policy enforces configuration rules, like requiring a specific region, and can even block a deployment outright if it doesn't comply. Resource locks add a separate layer of protection on individual resources, preventing accidental deletion or changes regardless of a user's normal permissions.

For cost, the Pricing calculator estimates what planned resources will cost, while the Total Cost of Ownership calculator compares an entire on-premises setup against running it in Azure. Tags make it possible to break spending down by department or project in Cost Management. Azure Advisor rounds this out with free, personalized recommendations across cost, security, reliability, operational excellence, and performance.

For health, Azure Monitor tracks your own resources — metrics, logs, and alerts — while Azure Service Health specifically reports on the health of the Azure platform itself, like a regional outage that isn't your fault at all.

You can manage all of this through the Azure portal, Cloud Shell (a browser-based command line with nothing to install), or Azure CLI/PowerShell installed locally for scripting — four ways to reach the same resources. Defining that configuration as Infrastructure as Code, using an ARM template, makes deployments repeatable and version-controlled instead of a one-off set of manual clicks. Two more services round out day-to-day governance: Microsoft Purview discovers and classifies sensitive data across your environment (including non-Azure sources), and Azure Arc extends familiar tools like Policy and RBAC to servers running outside Azure entirely.

A few more tools fill in the picture. The Azure portal, Azure CLI, and Azure PowerShell all go through Azure Resource Manager, and Copilot in Azure can explain options or draft commands, though you still validate its suggestions and Azure Policy still enforces your standards. Azure Arc projects servers, Kubernetes clusters, data services, and SQL Server running outside Azure into Resource Manager. In Cost Management, cost analysis breaks spend down by resource, subscription, or service; budget, credit, and department quota alerts cover different thresholds; and outbound data transfer is priced by billing zones, which are not availability zones. For health, Azure status shows global Azure health, Service Health shows events for the services and regions you use, and Resource Health shows one resource, while Application Insights availability tests catch an app that stops responding when no real users are around.
lessons.fundamentalsLabel: New to ongoing cloud operations? See the everyday analogy
lessons.fundamentals: This is the operational side of running any environment, cloud or not. Tags are like labeling supply closets by department so accounting knows who to bill. Azure Advisor is like a building inspector who walks through and flags things worth fixing, even though nothing's actively broken yet. And the Service Health versus Monitor distinction is the same as knowing whether the power went out because of your building's own wiring, or because the whole city grid went down — one you can fix yourself, the other you just have to wait out.
commonTraps: A Delete lock blocks deletion only — a Read-only lock is the one that also blocks modification.
Azure Service Health means Azure itself is having a problem. Azure Monitor means your own resources are.
Azure Advisor is free — it's not a paid add-on.
lessons.scenario: A finance team notices unexpected spend in one department's subscription. Because every resource there was tagged with a CostCenter value at creation, Cost Management can break the bill down by tag and pinpoint exactly which team is responsible — while Azure Advisor separately flags a handful of unused disks in that same subscription quietly adding to the bill.
lessons.onTheJob: Tags are the single biggest predictor of whether a monthly cost review is a five-minute glance or a multi-day investigation, and getting a team to apply them consistently, usually enforced through Azure Policy, is one of the few governance wins that pays for itself almost immediately. Azure Advisor's recommendations also tend to pile up and get ignored for months unless someone specifically owns acting on them, since flagging an idle disk and someone actually deleting it are two very different steps.

cheatSheet.heading: Exam-day strategy
points: Expect roughly 40–60 questions in about 45 minutes of exam time — a bit under a minute each on average. Budget more time for multi-part scenario questions and less for straight recall, rather than pacing every question identically.
Real scoring isn't a flat percentage of questions right (some count for more than others) — treat 75%+ as a safe buffer to aim for, not an exact threshold to just clear.

Flag anything you're unsure of and move on rather than stalling — a question later in the exam can sometimes jog a detail you needed earlier, and you get partial credit for nothing by running out of time on one question.
On multi-select ('choose N') questions, eliminate the options you're confident are wrong first; guessing among 2 plausible answers beats guessing among 4.
Your first read of a question is usually right — change an answer only when you find a specific detail you missed, not from general second-guessing.

cheatSheet.heading: Cloud service & deployment models
points: IaaS = rent infrastructure, you manage OS/runtime/apps (most control, most responsibility).
PaaS = platform managed for you, you manage just your app/data (e.g. Azure App Service).
SaaS = fully managed application, you just use it (e.g. Microsoft 365).
Public cloud = shared infra owned by the provider. Private cloud = dedicated to one org. Hybrid = both, connected.
CapEx (upfront capital purchase) vs. OpEx (ongoing operating expense) — cloud shifts spend from CapEx to OpEx.

cheatSheet.heading: Shared responsibility model
points: Physical security/hosts are always the provider's job, no matter which service model you use.
Moving IaaS → PaaS → SaaS shifts more responsibility to Microsoft and less to you.
Data classification and access management stay the customer's responsibility in every model.

cheatSheet.heading: Core architecture
points: Region = a set of datacenters with low-latency networking. Region pair = two regions in the same geography for disaster recovery.
Availability Zone = physically separate datacenters within a region (power/cooling/networking independent).
Availability Set = protects VMs in the same datacenter from a single hardware/rack failure, not a datacenter-wide outage.
Resource group = the container for related resources' lifecycle; a resource lives in exactly one resource group.
Management groups sit above subscriptions for organizing policy/access at scale.

cheatSheet.heading: Compute & networking essentials
points: VMs = most control, most management overhead. Containers = lighter, portable. Azure Functions = serverless, pay-per-execution.
VNet = your private network in Azure; subnets segment it; NSGs filter traffic in/out at the subnet or NIC level.
ExpressRoute = private dedicated connection to Azure (doesn't use the public internet). VPN Gateway = encrypted tunnel over the public internet.
Load Balancer = distributes traffic at layer 4 (TCP/UDP). Application Gateway = layer 7, understands HTTP (URL routing, WAF).

cheatSheet.heading: Storage & identity
points: Blob storage = unstructured data (files, media). Disk storage = VM disks. File storage = SMB file shares.
Storage redundancy: LRS (one datacenter) < ZRS (zone) < GRS (paired region, not readable) < RA-GRS (paired region, readable).
Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) = identity service; RBAC = who can do what on which resource; Conditional Access = under what conditions access is allowed.

Passwordless = Windows Hello for Business, Microsoft Authenticator, or FIDO2 security key. Entra Domain Services = managed domain (LDAP, Kerberos/NTLM); Entra Connect = sync of on-premises AD to Entra ID.
Blob tier minimum stays: Cool 30 days, Cold 90 days, Archive 180 days. Archive is per blob only and needs rehydration. Storage account names: 3 to 24 lowercase letters and numbers.
Service endpoint = optimized backbone route to a PaaS service; private endpoint = a private IP in your VNet. VPN Gateway: site-to-site, point-to-site, network-to-network; one gateway per VNet.

Region pairs are not universal: some regions (for example Poland Central) have none, and Brazil South is paired one way with South Central US. Sovereign regions: Azure Government and Azure operated by 21Vianet.
MFA = something you know + something you have/are — one of the most effective single controls against compromised passwords.

cheatSheet.heading: Cost & governance tools
